body:
# M1 blocker: validate compiled Aiken invariants with Blaster

Authority: operator instruction, 2026-09-12: “add blaster level invariants validation on the aiken code as M1 blocker”. Effective immediately for M1 acceptance and the integrated M1 release. This is additional to the existing code-the-design acceptance layers; it grants no conformance credit by itself.

Accountable owner: epic #18 owner, for the compiled-invariant inventory, executable verification artifact and integration into #80's strict publication gate. Epic #17 supplies the exact repaired validator artifacts and handles implementation defects through its existing serial writer. The milestone owner reviews the gates and independently challenges their negative controls. Existing staffing applies: GLM/Muse for mechanical work, no additional auditors or automatic fleet expansion.

## User story

As a Singular integrator, I can trace each applicable accepted Lean invariant through its readable Given/When/Then story to validation of the exact compiled Aiken program in the release, so that an implementation or compilation divergence prevents M1 acceptance.

## Required acceptance

1. Use a versioned inventory of every M1 validator title and every applicable invariant/required clause, derived from the full accepted Lean inventory. Preserve exact hypotheses, quantifiers, both directions of equivalences, vocabulary and refinement mappings. Unclassified applicability and missing rows remain debt. An exclusion requires a design-based rationale and milestone review; tool limitations do not justify exclusion.
2. Import the actual production-built UPLC through the pinned Blaster/PlutusCoreBlaster toolchain. Bind source commit and clean tree, actual compiler and dependency versions, blueprint and compiled-byte digests, exact validator titles, Plutus version, applied parameters and script identities, plus the explicit BuiltinSemanticsVariant justified for the target ledger. Never silently select a first title or a default semantics variant.
3. Validate the invariant against that imported program. A handwritten Lean model, Aiken source test, arbitrary receipt, successful import or bounded example alone cannot establish a quantified compiled-code claim. Record the checked domain and disposition separately: KERNEL-PROVED, SMT-VALID (no proof term), TESTED or UNPROVED. Finite CEK executions are TESTED; retain any remaining quantified obligation as debt.
4. Every assertion records ESTABLISHED, REFUTED or COULD-NOT-EVALUATE, with reproducible command, bound inputs, raw result/trace and evidence digests. Missing identity, unsupported builtin, opaque error, timeout, solver unknown, skipped or unreachable assertion is COULD-NOT-EVALUATE and blocks acceptance. Distinguish tooling failure from validator rejection.
5. Exercise valid controls and adversarial cases from the frozen design. Demonstrate discrimination with relevant source mutations rebuilt through the production compiler, prove the mutated bytes reached the evaluator, retain the intended REFUTED result and restore/reverify the baseline. The milestone owner supplies/checks independent gate controls under the existing no-extra-auditor ruling.
6. Preserve the settled ownerless registry contract: there is no registry owner role or latent owner/stake authority. Unmodeled End, migration, Sweep and Burning routes cannot restore inherited destructive authority. Legitimate application/name controllers, request/refund requirements and ordinary funding witnesses remain governed by their own clauses. Do not invent a ban on a registry creator funding or signing. Changes or ambiguity in Lean must be escalated through a concrete user story, never rewritten to satisfy code or tooling.
7. Supply a repository-owned reproducible command and CI integration. Extend #80's strict completion/publication gate with a separate per-obligation compiled-invariant debt category. Missing, stale, fabricated, skipped, unknown or failing evidence must prevent M1 acceptance/publication; unrelated green tests cannot offset it. Test removal of an inventory row/artifact, stale bytes/parameters/variant, false evidence and bypass/removal of the publication guard.
8. Publish human-readable Lean/story/compiled-check correspondence and the exact artifact evidence. M1 closes only when all required compiled-invariant obligations are discharged and all existing acceptance categories also reach zero. A bounded result is reported with its limits, never promoted to universal equivalence.

## Delivery order and fences

Prepare the inventory and toolchain/runner alongside current repairs. Bind definitive execution to the repaired ownerless schema and subsequent accepted candidate; rerun affected checks whenever source, parameters, toolchain or semantics change. Start with ownerless authority and supported-fold obligations as the first executable slice, then cover the full applicable M1 inventory. That first slice is not the denominator.

Keep #77's existing frozen gate and retained evidence intact; this is a separately versioned new M1 obligation. Do not interrupt current builds, add a second validator writer, weaken Lean, adopt Scalus, modify upstream MPFS, create an indexer, deploy to preprod or silently change the release version line. Existing bounded-release authority remains bounded and cannot be presented as completed M1. Ordinary independent docs publication retains its existing policy.

Read and apply aiken-blaster-verification and code-the-design. Before implementation, the epic owner records the issue, affected inventory, toolchain availability, first executable slice, worker ownership and terminal conditions. A toolchain obstacle remains an explicit M1 blocker; it is not an automatic waiver or permission to substitute model-only evidence.

Current result: REQUIRED / NOT YET ESTABLISHED. No Blaster run or compiled-invariant discharge is claimed by this commission.


## Parallel implementation authorized — 2026-09-12

The operator authorizes a Blaster implementation driver alongside the ongoing lifecycle and conformance repairs. Epic18 commissions an additional Muse driver in an isolated worktree for the compiled-artifact extraction/import/execution slice, covering both onchain and naming-onchain. The epic owner freezes the Lean invariant/refinement mappings and owns acceptance. Shared coverage-schema, CI and publication changes integrate serially through #80. Existing workers continue; no additional auditor is commissioned. This supersedes the earlier wait-for-an-existing-worker-to-finish scheduling hold. Preparation and instrumentation can run against an explicitly identified snapshot now; final evidence must bind the accepted repaired artifacts and all required debt remains blocking.

body:
Parent: #18. Preserved remainder of #68, which shipped seven of its eight rows.

## The obligation that remains uncovered

#68 required every `ProofStep` variant — `Branch`, `Fork`, `Leaf` — and `Neighbor` exercised by a
fold the validator accepted. `Branch` and `Leaf` are witnessed on chain. **`Fork` is not**, and this
issue exists so that requirement is not lost when #68's other seven rows merge.

Row CS07 is **unmarked**: `conformance/rows.json` says `uncovered`, no receipt exists, and nothing
claims `Fork` coverage.

## What is established

Two independently ground lone-root `Fork` absence proofs — `skip=1` and `skip=2` — each verified by
the pinned Haskell prover (`haskell-mts` at `13264a52b47e3a1f43a6ebeebd424a10f9e4466a`) against a
root identical to the cage's own, are **refused by the compiled validator** (state script
`874e476d7408de769e07a4ebf34f3c7379ebd7bd35ab8aad426b41d5`) with a bare `CekError` naming no reason.

Root agreement was established by execution: folds 1 and 2 were accepted by the same validator,
which recomputes the output root, so fold 3's proof was built against the chain's root.

Full bundle: `t68-serialization/handoffs/cs07-fork-finding.md` in the epic-18 runtime, six sections
with fact and inference labelled.

## What is not established

- whether **all** `Fork` steps are refused or only the lone-root shape — multi-step proofs ending in
  `Fork`, the shape the Aiken library's own vectors attest, were never exercised on chain;
- which side's encoding diverges — the bare `CekError` attributes nothing beyond the script;
- venue: both refusals were observed at build-time ledger evaluation, not as mempool rejections.

## Status

Escalated to the user as a story (epic-18 runtime `questions/Q-003`). A bounded investigation of the
exact failing proof bytes is authorized: isolate them through the pinned Aiken verifier and Haskell
prover, compare encoding and root reconstruction, use the library's vector shape or a multi-step
`Fork` as a discriminating control, with predictions committed before each probe runs.

**No library may be declared authoritative and no dependency may be updated by that investigation.**
It characterises the disagreement; it does not resolve it.

## Closing condition

This issue closes when `Fork` is exercised by a fold the validator accepted, or when a user ruling
settles the encoding correspondence and the resulting mapping is executed and checked. It does not
close on a report.

Until then CS07 stays in #80's coverage denominator as **unmet**, with the evidence limits above.


---

## Disposition updated — 2026-09-12

**The investigation-only hold above is superseded.** It is retained as history: it records what was
true when the encoding question was open, and the constraint it states — *no library may be declared
authoritative and no dependency updated* — still holds and is carried forward below.

**This is now an authorized implementation repair, not an open library choice.** The investigation
completed and its outcome was recorded in the epic-18 runtime as `A-005`, and in epic 17 as
`NOTE-016`:

- **Neither pinned library is the semantic authority.** Lean's omission of `ProofStep` constructors
  does not by itself establish a product ambiguity — a concrete Merkle encoding may be a
  *representation refinement* of already-modeled registry operations.
- Where the required abstract transition is unambiguous and the concrete implementation cannot
  realize it, that is an **implementation/refinement defect**, not a design question.
- **The user is not asked to choose a library merely because two implementations disagree.**

### Ownership

**Epic 17** owns the product repair and its serial integration — live producer:
`ticket-81/commit-owner`, branch `fix/fork-absence-insert-81`. **Epic 18** owns consumer replay and
the #68/#81 coverage disposition.

### Constraints on the repair

Bind the existing failure to **all** accepted abstract preconditions, preserve the **exact
absent-key obligation**, and deliver a local repair with **causal controls**. No library-as-authority
decision, no proof-shape exclusion, no dependency refresh, and no repetition of the completed probe
campaign.

### What this does not do

**#68 and #81 both stay open.** No CS07 success is claimed, no conformance row is relabelled, and
every historical finding above is preserved — including the falsified prediction P-B (present-key
`Fork` ACCEPTED, `4c5c4e5ac8…`) that narrowed the defect to the `excluding()` path.

body:
## User story

As a Singular user and contributor, I want every Lean contract invariant checked against the actual implementation at more than one test layer, so that a proved model and passing demo cannot conceal a different deployed behavior.

## Problem

The repository checks109 exported Lean contract theorems (41 generic,17 naming,43 lifecycle,8 wire) and finite simulator replay, but has no theorem-to-implementation acceptance-coverage ratchet. The retrospective review found owner-only folding, missing real registration/representative issuance, and substituted retirement effects despite those checks passing. Proof debt and implementation conformance debt are different.

## Deliverable

A runnable, CI-integrated acceptance layer in `conformance/` that derives the authoritative obligation inventory from fixed Lean, maps each invariant to a user story and at least two distinct executable implementation checks, reports exact missing/insufficient/stale/failing obligations, prevents regression per obligation, and refuses full completion until all required coverage and results are complete.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Reconcile all109 public contract statements by qualified name and statement digest; discover additional declarations/transition obligations and report anything unclassified. Do not silently omit helpers, conjuncts, refusals or quantified domains.
- [ ] Each behavioral invariant maps to a generated property/state-machine test against actual implementation and a distinct story/integration test across its relevant production boundary. Two wrappers, duplicated assertions, or model/simulator replay alone do not qualify.
- [ ] State-machine checks generate reachable command sequences, compare pre/postconditions and observations after each command to fixed Lean semantics, include adversarial/refused actions, and print replay seeds plus minimized counterexamples. Shrinking preserves prerequisites; discarded/unreached domains do not pass.
- [ ] Mapping fields identify user story, declaration/source digest, clauses/preconditions, implementation entry points, test IDs/layers, commands, result/provenance identities and discrimination controls. PASS is computed from selected executed checks, never typed.
- [ ] Machine-readable and readable reports separate unmapped, insufficient-layer, unclassified, unexecuted/stale, failing and invalid-control debt. Report initial counts honestly; a missing register is not proof that all existing behavior is untested.
- [ ] PR ratchet compares per-obligation coverage to the protected base; debt cannot move between rows to hide regression, theorem removal cannot shrink the denominator, and automatic baseline increases are forbidden.
- [ ] A distinct full-completion gate exits nonzero unless every required obligation has sufficient current passing evidence and valid controls. Wire it into milestone/release-completion acceptance. Ordinary repair PRs can reduce an explicit nonzero baseline without claiming the project complete.
- [ ] Demonstrate rejection of deleted mappings, disabled/unselected tests, duplicate layers, stale evidence, unreachable/vacuous generators, weakened invariants, and wrong results relabelled expected.
- [ ] First behavioral mappings cover #79 permissionless folding/insert-only withdrawal, #77 real registration/representative identity and the connected retirement path as their code becomes available. Current broken code must produce genuine RED evidence; no model rewrite or expectation waiver.
- [ ] Update the constitution/PR acceptance instructions to require this coverage record and zero-debt completion, coordinating shared paths through the milestone owner. No change to accepted Lean semantics, proofs' assumptions, or invariant domain.

## Ownership and dependencies

Parent #18 owns the coverage layer and dedicated workflow; #17 owns validator repairs. Existing GLM/Muse mechanical contributors and direct owner gate review; no extra auditor fleet. This is required acceptance work before claiming the milestone complete or the complete naming journey ready for preprod. The current Lean model is fixed; real ambiguity goes to the user BEFORE semantic edits.

## Evidence limits

A green mapping checker is not semantic evidence. Counts close only when the tests actually exercise and discriminate the intended implementation behavior. Random testing supplies conformance evidence, not a universal proof of implementation correctness. Keep Lean proof debt, simulator replay and actual implementation acceptance results separate.


## User amendment: Lean owns the BDD language

Lean must also govern the domain nomenclature used by stories and tests. Every theorem obligation has a traceable Given/When/Then representation preserving its quantified inputs/preconditions, modeled action or observation, and full conclusion/effects/refusals. Bind exact Lean symbols and statement digests; reject missing or ambiguous vocabulary mappings. A scenario file is not execution evidence and a single example does not discharge a quantified property. The BDD contract feeds the distinct property/state-machine and integration layers already required above.

Include missing/stale BDD mappings in the coverage ratchet; do not count them as implemented tests until actual checks execute and discriminate defects. Preserve all semantics and invariants.

The user has an existing BDD/DSL repository. Its URL/path has been requested and is pending. Inspect it BEFORE choosing DSL syntax, parsing/bindings, runner architecture or a framework. Do not assume Gherkin/Cucumber or invent a competing language. Inventory and existing implementation repairs continue independently.


## Human correspondence and BDD candidate evaluation (operator amendment, 2026-09-11)

The governing skill is [code-the-design](https://github.com/paolino/llm-settings/blob/main/shared/skills/code-the-design/SKILL.md). Humans must be able to match Lean and acceptance: publish a clause-by-clause view pairing each exact theorem, faithful plain-language reading and Given/When/Then using the same domain vocabulary, with pinned sources and actual test evidence. Mark extra assumptions, interpretation and missing behavior explicitly. Present a representative rendered story for operator review before scaling a new DSL across the suite.

The forgotten repository was found: [paolino/tasty-bdd](https://github.com/paolino/tasty-bdd/tree/f55494c9b917ec12b4d01e506694b1a5c3b41b56); [paolino/haskell-bdd](https://github.com/paolino/haskell-bdd) is a distinct older fork. Evaluate tasty-bdd as a candidate, not an adopted dependency. Source inspection confirms typed Given/When/Then combinators and Tasty integration, but no Lean vocabulary or theorem mapping. Its source exports testBehavior/testBehaviorF (the README testBdd name is stale), and assertion-free scenarios are representable. Current-toolchain compatibility has not been established.

Bound the evaluation to a representative real implementation story: positive and deliberately failing executions under the existing Nix toolchain, assertion failure propagation, resource cleanup and a readable Lean/acceptance pairing. Record whether the library plus a thin domain adapter serves that purpose before suite-wide adoption; do not refresh unrelated locks or change accepted semantics. Finding the repository supersedes the missing-URL hold. Library feasibility, story generation and ratchet installation do not discharge implementation-coverage debt.


## Evaluation source update (operator, 2026-09-12)

Use [lambdasistemi/tasty-bdd](https://github.com/lambdasistemi/tasty-bdd) for the BDD evaluation and any subsequent authorized integration. At this update its default branch points to f55494c9b917ec12b4d01e506694b1a5c3b41b56, identical to the previously inspected paolino/tasty-bdd revision. Preserve earlier evidence provenance. The repository change does not settle library adoption or replace the required human-readable Lean/acceptance review and real implementation tests.


## M1 blocker: compiled Aiken invariants (operator, 2026-09-12)

- [ ] Complete #87: validate every applicable M1 invariant against the exact production-built Aiken UPLC using the pinned Blaster/CEK toolchain, preserving the accepted Lean clauses and readable Given/When/Then correspondence.
- [ ] Bind candidate, compiler, blueprint, parameters and explicit builtin semantics; retain discriminating rebuilt-source controls and reproducible evidence. Missing, unsupported, unknown, stale or failing results remain blocking debt. Model-only proofs and finite executions do not establish quantified compiled-code claims.
- [ ] Enforce this separate per-obligation debt in #80 strict M1 completion and integrated publication. It supplements the existing two implementation layers; no M1 closure or integrated M1 release until all required obligations are discharged. Epic18 owns verification/gate integration; epic17 supplies repaired artifacts and implementation fixes. Existing no-extra-auditor staffing remains in force.

Full acceptance contract: https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/issues/87.

Two clear implementation defects in the imported partition contradict unchanged
Singular semantics. A retrospective Lean audit found the first; building the
retirement path found the second. Both block every permissionlessness and
end-to-end claim in M1.

Per the repository constitution (Principle I), imported code and pinned
dependencies carry the same obligation as code written here. These are repairs
owed, not inherited exemptions.

## P1 user story

As a folder — anyone at all — I want to apply pending requests to the registry
without anyone's permission, and as the holder of a retired name I want to be
unable to take it back, so that the registry is the permissionless, permanent
structure its model and its front page describe.

## Defect 1 — every fold requires the registry owner's signature

`onchain/validators/state.ak`'s `spend` runs `expect validateOwnership(state, tx)`
**before dispatching any redeemer**, and `onchain/validators/shared.ak`'s
`validateOwnership` requires `has(extra_signatories, owner)` — plus a
stake-script withdrawal when one is configured. Every state spend, therefore
every `Modify`, therefore every fold, needs the registry owner.

Lean's `.fold` (`lean/Singular/Model.lean`) checks only `nativeSpend`, net mint
equality, and the representative/application mint witnesses when the
corresponding net is nonzero. **There is no owner and no privileged folder.**
`README.md` states the same as product intent: "There is no owner to sign, no
privileged actor."

The imported tree documents its owner requirement as its own architecture
(`onchain/validators/types.ak`): "The `owner` field determines who can perform
`Modify` and `End` operations." MPFS is an owner-moderated cage; Singular is not.
The old imported architecture is not the oracle for Singular's behavior.

**Repair:** the modeled fold path must not require the owner. `End` keeps its
ownership requirement, and every structural, mint, proof and request check on the
`Modify` path is retained. Scope the change from the full validator paths, not
from an assumption that one clause is involved.

## Defect 2 — a retirement request can be withdrawn

`onchain/validators/request.ak`'s `validateRetract` requires only the request
owner's signature and phase-2 timing. It does not look at the request operation,
so an `Update` request — which is what a retirement is — is retractable.

Lean forbids this twice: `step .withdraw` throws `withdraw-insert-only` for any
request that is not an insert (`insertNative` requires `r.operation == .insert`),
and `step .escape` throws `completion-only-custody`.

**Repair:** restrict retraction to insert requests. Everything else about
`Retract` — the owner signature, the phase-2 window, the state-token binding —
is retained.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A valid fold is accepted **without** the registry owner among the required
      signers, submitted by a party with no privileged relationship to the
      registry, on a real devnet.
- [ ] Negative control for defect 1: the same fold with a defect in any other
      modeled precondition is still refused. The repair must not have disabled
      authorization generally — enumerate the checks on the `Modify` path and
      show each still refuses.
- [ ] `End` still requires the state owner, and its refusal without that
      signature is executed.
- [ ] An `Update` request cannot be retracted, executed as a real spend attempt
      refused by the request validator for that reason.
- [ ] Negative control for defect 2: an **insert** request can still be retracted
      by its owner in the phase-2 window, executed. The repair must not have
      removed withdrawal generally — `LC01` cancellation behavior is preserved.
- [ ] The imported provenance baseline stays
      `34a5bfbb8cca2cb1911b7060d0e61db28ba21e83`. A separate, explicit, reviewed
      patch records the local repair, and the provenance gate **reconstructs
      baseline + that exact patch** and rejects any unlisted drift. The baseline
      hashes and lock files are preserved. The check is not disabled and expected
      hashes are not merely replaced with current bytes.
- [ ] Script identities are derived from the actual pinned compilation, the
      resulting bytes are reviewed, and the new identities are propagated to
      builders and release manifests.
- [ ] Every existing runner still passes: `li01`, `li-refusals`, `naming-rows`,
      `recovery-rows`, `retirement-rows`, `journey`, the devnet E2E suite.
- [ ] Mutation census with no survivor over both repaired paths.

Parent #17. Epic 17 owns these source paths for this repair (`A-002`); #18 owns
the discriminating consumer gates and must not edit them concurrently. Prerequisite
for #77 and for the retirement completion path.

No upstream repository edit and no dependency refresh. No change to `lean/` or
any frozen contract path — semantics, invariants, corpus expectations and
protocol requirements are fixed inputs. No global disabling of authorization, no
dropping of structural or mint checks, no removal of a negative control, no
redefinition of a row. If a genuine model contradiction appears, it is escalated
as a user story **before** any semantic edit.

Parent: #18. Prepared release target: `handoffs/preprod-onboarding-release.md` (milestone runtime).

## The user story

**As a new Singular contributor, I want to download one versioned artifact, configure my own test
wallet, and execute a documented journey against a persistent shared test network, so that I can
learn and extend the real system without reconstructing the factory's worktrees or genesis
fixtures.**

## The concrete blocker this slice removes

Every runner in this repository starts a **local devnet**: `onchain-release/README.md` says each
runner starts its own node; the journey runners call `withCardanoNode` / `genesisDir` /
`devnetMagic`; `li01/Main.hs` derives the canonical seed from genesis-wallet UTxOs. **None of them
reaches preprod by changing a network flag**, and none of them can, because they assume they own the
chain and hold its genesis keys.

So this slice builds the missing mode, in `conformance/` only.

## Scope

1. **External-node mode for the conformance runner.** Connect to a node/provider given by
   configuration rather than spawned; verify **network magic 1**; query live protocol parameters and
   use them rather than devnet constants. The local-devnet path keeps working unchanged — this is an
   additional mode, not a replacement.
2. **Joiner-owned wallet.** Key material supplied by the joiner, kept local, never a devnet genesis
   key. Check funds and collateral before attempting anything and fail with a diagnostic that names
   what is missing rather than a balance exception. Faucet funding is the joiner's step, documented.
3. **Canonical deployment manifest — format and verifier, not a published claim.** A manifest binding
   release revision, Lean revision, network, seed outRef, applied script hashes, policy IDs and
   bootstrap transactions, with a command that authenticates an artifact against it.
4. **The runbook**, `docs/consumer-onboarding.md` plus its speech companion: download, verify
   checksum, configure the node, create the wallet, fund it, authenticate the manifest, run, and
   what each expected output looks like — including confirmation waits, diagnostic failures and
   rerun behavior.

## What this slice must NOT claim

- **No preprod deployment, no published canonical identity, no funded wallet, no endpoint
  selection.** This prepares the capability; it does not deploy. No credentials are provisioned.
- **The canonical identity claim is blocked** until the canonical-identity ambiguity is ruled by the
  user (epic runtime `questions/Q-002`, story 1). The manifest **format** and its verifier can be
  built now; publishing an identity as canonical cannot.
- The naming register→resolve→recover→retire journey belongs to **epic 17**. Do not implement it and
  do not stand in for its missing transitions.
- No indexer, no dependency update, no parallel implementation, no factoring of the imported
  partitions.

## Order of evidence

First the connected journey against a **clean devnet in external-node mode** with realistically
queried parameters and the current negative controls — this proves the mode without needing a shared
network. Preprod execution comes after, against the exact candidate, and is not part of this slice's
acceptance.

## Acceptance

- [ ] the runner connects to an externally supplied node, verifies magic 1, and uses live queried protocol parameters
- [ ] a joiner-supplied wallet works end to end, with no genesis key anywhere in the path, and missing funds/collateral produce a named diagnostic
- [ ] the manifest format is specified and a verifier authenticates an artifact against it
- [ ] `docs/consumer-onboarding.md` and its speech companion pass the presentation gate
- [ ] the local-devnet path is unchanged and still green
- [ ] every still-unready portion is marked explicitly, naming what blocks it
- [ ] `offchain/`, `onchain/`, `naming-onchain/` byte-unchanged; any needed change there is reported, not made

## Goal

The retrospective Lean audit found that no naming key has ever had a registry
entry, and that the "representative" every merged slice carries is a stand-in
token under the **application** policy rather than the representative policy the
model binds. Both are blocking coverage gaps (`R03`, and the representative half
of `R05`).

This slice makes the representative real and gets a name into the registry as
`Active`, which every later behavior reads.

## P1 user story

As an integrator authenticating a name, I want the NFT I check to be the one the
registry's representative policy minted for that key and incarnation, and I want
the registry to actually say the key is active, so that what I authenticate is
what the contract binds.

## What Lean requires

`lean/Singular/Model.lean`:

- `representative s key` is under `config.representativePolicy`, scoped by the
  entry's **incarnation** — not a canonical address, which is what the stand-in
  used;
- `step .createInsert` requires the request's token to be
  `insertAsset r.proposal`, minted under the application policy and binding the
  exact proposal;
- `foldOne .insert` refuses `occupied-key` when the entry is occupied, checks the
  approval scope against the incarnation, checks `representative-identity` and
  the certified output, then sets the entry `.active` and emits a `+1`
  representative delta that the mint must match under `sameNet`.

`naming-onchain/validators/representative.ak` already exists and is pinned;
`MintRepresentative` requires the application spend's redeemer to be
`Fold { representatives }` naming exactly the tokens moved, so the mint is only
reachable through a real fold. That coupling is what the stand-in bypassed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The representative is minted under `representative.representative.mint`,
      with an asset name carrying `(registry, key, incarnation)` as Lean scopes
      it. No application-policy stand-in remains in any row.
- [ ] The application policy's mint purpose gains the insert-approval arm that
      binds the exact proposal — the seam
      `offchain/naming-correspondence.md` has recorded as unrealised since #52.
- [ ] An insert request is created and **folded**, on a real devnet, so the
      registry entry for the key reaches `.active` and the representative is
      minted `+1` by that fold. The root change is read back from the chain.
- [ ] The resulting record is the one `#62`'s recovery and `#66`'s retirement
      rows operate on: both runners pass against a genuinely folded name, not a
      fixture.
- [ ] `occupied-key` is executed as a **consequence of the fold**: a second
      insert for the same active key is refused, with the control that an insert
      for a free key succeeds in the same run.
- [ ] **The owner-signature divergence is recorded, not hidden.** The fold is a
      state spend, so under the frozen imported partition it needs the registry
      owner's signature, while Lean's `.fold` requires only `nativeSpend` plus
      mint witnesses. Every narration line and the correspondence record must say
      so. No line may imply permissionlessness.
- [ ] Mutation census with no survivor over the new mint arm and the fold path.
- [ ] Every existing runner still passes: `recovery-rows`, `retirement-rows`,
      `naming-rows`, `li-refusals`, `li01`.

## Dependencies

Parent #17, after #66. Root has authorized the inherited naming/registry
integration scope for this repair (`A-001`). Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

## Out of scope, and why

Retirement's modeled Update request and the `.update` fold into `Over` are
**blocked** pending the user ruling on `Q-002` — both need one-clause changes
inside the byte-exact imported partition (`state.ak`'s owner requirement on
every fold, `request.ak`'s operation-blind `Retract`). Nothing in this slice
touches `onchain/`.

The custody script and the widened mint arm stay exactly as merged. They exist
to work around the substrate and are retired only if the connected retirement
path lands.

No upstream repository edit, no dependency refresh, no factoring, no extra
auditor.

## Goal

Retirement can be *initiated* on a ledger (#66): either authorized route moves
the representative into a completion-only custody script. **Nothing has ever
spent that custody UTxO**, so the three claims that make retirement permanent
are still untested — that anyone can complete it, that nobody can undo it, and
that the key never becomes registrable again.

| row | accepted | what the ledger must show |
|---|---|---|
| `LT04-retirement-completes` | yes | an **unsigned** transaction spends the custody UTxO, burns the representative exactly once, and moves the registry entry to `Over` |
| `LT07-retirement-withdrawal-refused` | no | a real spend of the custody UTxO that tries to take the representative back out — refused, by the custody script, executing |
| `LO01-retirement-pending-visible` | — | after initiation and before completion the state is observably `pending`: representative alive in custody, record gone, **no live naming resolution** |
| `LO02-retirement-over-visible` | — | after completion the state is observably `retired`: representative burned, registry entry `Over`, still no live resolution |
| `LX01-re-registration-after-over-refused` | no | a fresh registration of the same key is queued, and folding it is refused on `occupied-key` — the absence proof cannot be produced against a root whose key holds `Over` |

## P1 user story

As anyone at all I finish a retirement somebody else authorized, and neither the
holder nor the quorum nor I can undo it; and the name can never be claimed
again by anyone, including its former holder.

## The transitions, from the accepted model

`lean/Singular/NamingLifecycle.lean`:

- `finishRetirement` folds the pending request and burns the representative
  (`-1`), with `executingWitness` exactly `nativeSpend` and `representativeMint`
  — **no required signers, no quorum signers**. Completion is permissionless;
  a row that needs a signature has not shown that;
- `refuseRetirementWithdrawal` throws `retirement-withdrawal-refused` for any
  pending retirement, unconditionally;
- the `LO` rows are authenticated reads returning `pending` and `retired`;
- `LX01` queues a second registration successfully and its **fold** is refused
  with `occupied-key`. Queueing is not the refusal; folding is.

## Creating an output executes no receiving script

`LT08` in #66 proved the `Retire` spend refuses a wrong custody destination.
That says nothing about the custody script, which has never run: Cardano
executes a script when its output is **spent**. So every row here must spend a
custody UTxO that a real `LT01` or `LT02` transaction created in the same run.
A fixture output built to look like custody proves nothing about custody.

## `LX01` needs the registry, and the registry machinery already exists

This is the row that has no precedent in this epic. `Over` is a value in the
authenticated registry, not a property of the application output, so `LX01`
cannot be shown at the application validator alone.

Epic 16 built every piece needed, in `offchain/journey/li01/Main.hs`: boot a
cage on a real devnet, submit an insert request, **prove a key absent against
the root read back from the chain**, apply the request, and prove it present.
`LX01` is that machinery pointed at a key whose entry holds `Over`: the absence
proof that folding requires cannot be produced, and the fold is refused.

Reuse it. Do not write a second trie implementation, and do not compare a proof
against a root this runner derived itself — compare against the root read back
from the chain, the discipline `li01` already follows.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `LT04` executes with **no signature of any kind**: the transaction's
      required signers are empty, and it is submitted by a party that is neither
      the controller nor any quorum member. The representative is observed
      burned on chain and the registry entry observed at `Over`.
- [ ] `LT07` is a **real spend attempt** of a live custody UTxO, refused by the
      custody script with a phase-2 `PlutusFailure` naming that script's hash —
      not a transaction that was never built, and not a phase-1 refusal.
- [ ] `LO01` and `LO02` are read from the chain at the two distinct points and
      are observably different from each other, and neither yields a live naming
      resolution. State plainly what "no live resolution" is checked against.
- [ ] `LX01` queues a second registration for the retired key against a real
      registry, and the fold is refused because the absence proof cannot stand
      against the chain-read root. The refusal is attributed to `occupied-key`,
      not to an incidental error.
- [ ] A control shows the same registration **succeeding** for a key that is not
      retired, so `LX01`'s refusal is attributable to `Over` and not to the
      harness being unable to register anything.
- [ ] Controls: an accepted row made to fail, and a refusal matched against an
      impossible reason, both fail the run after executing rows.
- [ ] A mutation census over the custody script and the completion path leaves
      **no survivor**.
- [ ] `recovery-rows`, the retirement rows from #66, `naming-rows`,
      `li-refusals` and `li01` all still pass.
- [ ] `docs/recovery-retirement.md` and `offchain/naming-correspondence.md`
      record what runs today, and state which witnesses
      (`representativeMint`, `nativeSpend`, `authenticatedRead`) this slice
      realised and which remain intended-but-unproven.

## Dependencies

Parent #17, after #66. Shares the custody script, the application validator and
the runner, so it is serialized behind it. Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

## Non-goals

No change to `onchain/`. No quorum rotation, takeover or `Close`. No naming
`Delete`, release or reuse — generic `Delete` stays exactly as the consumer
requires it, and nothing here may make the **generic** path refuse it. No death
or inactivity oracle. Retirement stops name-based resolution; it cannot stop
payments to a raw address somebody already saved, and no row may suggest
otherwise.

|---|---|---|

The table above records what was expected when this issue was filed. It is kept unchanged as that
record. Since then the operator ruled that **Singular has no registry-owner role whatsoever** —

Parent: #18. Follows #63, which established the harness and the first four generic rows.

## What a person can run when this is done

```
nix run ./conformance#conformance -- run CS01 CS02 CS03 CS04 CS05 CS06 CS07 CS08
```

## Why these rows

Issue #18 requires the actual Haskell serialization and transaction-construction boundary: *"matching
datum/redeemer/parameter encoding and compiled execution evidence"*, and states that a same-stack
emulator or source-language-independent Plutus output does **not** establish application
compatibility. These eight rows are that boundary.

The point of CS01 is the one most easily faked: a round-trip test proves a codec is self-consistent,
which is worth nothing about the ledger. The claim that must be executed is that each Haskell
encoding matches the **compiled blueprint's own declared schema** — constructor index and field
order — and then that the compiled validator accepts what Haskell produced.

## Rows

| row | requirement | expected |
|---|---|---|
| CS01 | Every `ToData`/`FromData` instance in `Cardano.MPFS.Cage.Types` round-trips **and** its constructor index and field order match the compiled blueprint's declared schema | accept, checked against the blueprint, not against itself |
| CS02 | Datum bytes constructed in Haskell and submitted are read back from the chain identical | accept, byte-compare submitted vs chain-observed |
| CS03 | Each `UpdateRedeemer` constructor — `End` 0, `Contribute` 1, `Modify` 2, `Retract` 3, `Sweep` 4 — is exercised by a submitted transaction the validator executed | accept, one executing witness per constructor |
| CS04 | A redeemer at a wrong constructor index | refuse, attributed to the script |
| CS05 | Each `RequestAction` (`Update` 0, `Rejected` 1) and `MintRedeemer` (`Minting` 0, `Migrating` 1, `Burning` 2) constructor executed, or recorded unreachable with its reason | accept, or an explicit recorded gap |
| CS06 | Script parameter application: parameter count and encoding published; the applied hash derived in Haskell equals the on-chain address for every parameterized script | accept |
| CS07 | Each `ProofStep` variant (`Branch` 0, `Fork` 1, `Leaf` 2) and `Neighbor` exercised by a fold the validator accepted | accept |
| CS08 | `OnChainTokenState`'s six fields survive a chain round trip with `stake_script` both `None` and `Some` | accept |

CS01 and CS06 need no node. The rest do.

`Migrating` may be genuinely unreachable against the imported partition. If so, CS05 records it as a
gap with the reason read from the validator — never as a pass, and never omitted.

CS07 needs tries deep enough to force `Fork` and multi-step `Branch` proofs; a single-key trie only
produces `Leaf`. Build the trie to the shape each variant requires.

Owned: `conformance/**` and `docs/consumer-conformance.md`. `offchain/`, `onchain/`,

Closes #57.

Fifteen merged slices of this epic were reachable only by cloning the repository and
running Nix: the blueprints, Singular's naming validators, the codec, the journey, and
all eighteen contract rows. An integrator could obtain none of it.

## What is packaged

The existing machinery now assembles a **second** archive alongside the documentation
one — `singular-onchain-<version>.tar.gz` — carrying:

- both compiled blueprints, and **both identity layers** with their parameter counts
  (the imported partition and Singular's own naming scripts);
- the journey and row runners, and the documented commands to invoke them;
- the vendored v0.2.0 wire fixtures with their provenance;
- a checksum manifest over every member.

The documentation archive is **untouched**, still byte-identical to epic 15's v0.2.0
asset (`acbabdf5…`). Two archives, not one absorbing the other.

## The blueprints are provably the pinned ones

They enter packaging as **pure derivation inputs** built from the carried sources and
verified against the committed identity manifests — not store paths trusted from a
shell variable. No flake lock changed, and nothing evaluates across a flake boundary:
each sub-flake resolves against its own lock, which is what the two-flake split was
for.

## Reproduction from the artifact, not from this repository

| step | result |
|---|---|
| extracted to `/tmp/t57-repro/extracted`, outside every worktree | — |
| `sha256sum --check SHA256SUMS` over 134 members | exit 0 |
| both identity layers verified **from the archive alone** against its carried blueprints | PASS |
| wire-vector suite re-run from the extraction, 17 checks over 4 vectors | PASS |

Every command came from the artifact's own `README.md`. Reproducing from the
repository would not have satisfied this and was not done — the point is that someone
who has cloned nothing can confirm the scripts are the ones the identities describe.

## What the release says it is not

Marked **epic-scoped**, not the milestone or product artifact. It states that recovery
and retirement belong to epic 17, and that its row evidence is **finite fixture
execution** rather than a claim about arbitrary transactions.

## Publication

The pipeline publishes from a tag; this PR contains the machinery and the proof it
works. The tag follows the merge, and the published artifact gets the same
reproduction check applied to the bytes an integrator would actually download.

`actionlint` clean on all three workflows.

Closes #49.

The four v0.2.0 wire vectors exist twice in this repository: vendored into
`offchain/naming/src/Naming/Wire/Vectors.hs` with their provenance, and in epic 15's
merged corpus at `lean/lifecycle-corpus.json`.

That duplication is deliberate. A consumed contract is **pinned** — reading the live
file would make Singular's encoding follow whatever that file becomes, which is the
opposite of consuming an accepted release. But it left a blind spot: if epic 15
revised its corpus, **nothing said so**, and the vendored copy would keep passing
against bytes the contract no longer ships.

## What the check does, and deliberately does not do

It compares the two copies and **reports divergence without resolving it**. The pin
stays; a human decides whether to adopt a moved contract. Re-pointing the suite at the
live corpus would have been the wrong fix — it would silently change what Singular
claims to implement.

Baseline: 14/14 identical, exit 0.

## It fires from both directions

| control | result |
|---|---|
| one byte changed in epic 15's corpus | exit 1, names `WR01` with both hex values |
| one byte changed in the vendored copy | exit 1, names `WD01` |
| a row missing | exit 1 |
| a row added | exit 1 |

Testing only our own copy would have missed the case the check exists for — the
contract moving underneath us.

## `lean/**` joins the trigger paths

Without it a corpus-only revision would not trigger this workflow at all, and the
drift check would never run on precisely the change it was built to catch. That is the
difference between a check that exists and a check that fires.

`actionlint` clean on the workflow — per the lesson from the previous slice, where a
swallowed newline made `mpfs.yml` invalid and silently disabled every epic-16 check on
a pull request while nothing reported a failure.

## Scope

No vendored byte changed, the pinned release is untouched, and epic 15's corpus is
read but never written.

body:
Closes #50.

`LI01` proved canonical initialization can be done. These seven attempts establish
what happens when it is done wrongly — each substituting one element of the binding,
otherwise well formed, with the script integrity hash re-sealed so the refusal is
attributable.

## Three enforcement mechanisms, not one

**Validators refuse five.** `LI02` an alternate seed that is not an input; `LI04` a
substituted registry failing exact-quantity; `LI05` a substituted application policy
failing its own address discipline; `LI07` a substituted representative policy that
cannot ride along; `LI08` a substituted validator script that cannot bootstrap. All
phase-2, each matched on its reason.

**The ledger refuses one.** `LI06` runs after a real `LI01`: the canonical seed is
spent, so replaying it is refused before any script runs. Reported as ledger-level,
not dressed up as a validator decision.

**`LI03` is not refused at all — and that is the finding.**

## The finding

The frozen bootstrap checks every condition **relative to the redeemer's own seed**
and has no canonical-seed allowlist. So an internally consistent rival registry from
a second seed is **accepted** by the ledger (`tx=6bad8f09…`).

It cannot be mistaken for the canonical registry. The registry token name is SHA-256
of the seed's outRef, so the rival carries a different name — `0xe8cd6e40…` against
the canonical `0x38bde245…` — and `LI06` shows the canonical seed can never be
consumed twice. **There is exactly one canonical registry, forever.**

The row therefore asserts what is true and checkable: the rival accepted, its name
distinct, and the canonical registry unaffected, read back from the chain. It does not
assert a refusal the ledger cannot produce.

## Why the alternative was rejected

Giving the bootstrap a canonical-seed allowlist would mean parameterizing or forking
the imported state script. That crosses the custody fence established in #19, moves
pinned identities again, and buys no safety against something already unmistakable.
Recutting `LI03` into a refusable shape was also rejected: the only construction the
frozen partition refuses is indistinguishable from `LI02`, so the row would have
tested the seed check twice and the registry substitution never.

## The record is corrected where it was wrong

`naming-correspondence.md` previously said uniqueness "is enforced by *spending*" the
seed. That holds for the canonical seed — `LI02` and `LI06` confirm it — and **does
not** hold against rivals from other seeds. The correction sits inline in the
`canonicalSeed` row, not in a footnote, and the record now enumerates the three
mechanisms above.

## Controls and limits

Both controls fail as required: an attempt that is actually canonical, and a refusal
matched against the wrong reason. After the attempts the canonical state reads back
unchanged. No validator was touched and no refusal weakened.

Seven fixture attempts are not a statement about arbitrary transactions. The model's
`LI03` refusal is not realisable as a ledger refusal — a contract-level observation
being carried to the milestone owner.

Closes #56.

Every row in this epic had been proved at model level by epic 15 or at Aiken level by
the naming validators. **None of `LM` or `LC` had touched a ledger.** All ten now do.

## The rows, on a devnet

| row | outcome |
|---|---|
| `WR01` | refund recorded at request time round-trips on chain |
| `LM01` | accepted — **and** control, commitment and quorum read back from the chain through the merged codec and compared field by field |
| `LM02` / `LM03` / `LM04` | refused phase-2, reasons matched: missing controller signature, altered preserved field, altered quorum |
| `LC01` | accepted — **and** the approval burned once in `a11376a1…` then verified absent |
| `LC02` | redirected refund refused |
| `LC03` | Insert approval alone does not authorize cancellation |
| `LC04` | refused **after a real fold** |
| `LC06` | replaying `LC01`'s exact transaction refused by the ledger — "All inputs are spent" |

After the refusals the authenticated state reads back unchanged. Both controls fail
as required: a row whose transaction is actually valid, and a refusal matched against
the wrong reason.

`LC06` is a **ledger-level** refusal, not a validator decision — the input is already
spent, so nothing reaches a script. That is arguably the strongest form of the
guarantee, and it is reported as what it is rather than folded in with the phase-2
refusals.

## Executing the rows found a validator that could not be used

`LC01` was refused phase-2 by the application script's **mint** purpose while its
**spend** purpose accepted it. The two purposes of one script disagreed: the spend
path demanded a burn the mint path refused, so no real cancellation could be built.

**The 59 Aiken checks in #52 passed over this.** They exercise one purpose at a time
against a constructed script context; a transaction presents both purposes in one
context and requires them to agree. No per-purpose suite asks that question.

The mint handler is repaired with two tests, and the script's identity changes
accordingly — `b180c934…` → `e3576e3d…` — recorded in the manifest alongside the code
change rather than arriving as a regenerated hash.

## What now enforces purpose agreement

The new CI job runs these rows on a devnet on every change. A transaction is the only
thing that presents both purposes at once, so the row *is* the composition test;
per-purpose Aiken tests sit underneath it. Where a constructed test and a real
execution can both cover an invariant, the real execution cannot be constructed
wrongly.

## Limits

Ten fixture rows executing is not a statement about arbitrary transactions. Recovery
(`LR`) and retirement (`LO`) belong to epic 17. The `LI` refusals (#50) and the
versioned release (#57) remain.

## Goal

Epic 16 owes a versioned, retrievable on-chain release. Everything it has built so
far is reachable only by cloning the repository and running Nix: the blueprint, the
naming validators, the codec, the journey, `LI01`, and the contract rows. An
integrator cannot obtain any of it.

A-003 settled the ownership question: this epic ships through the repository's
existing release machinery and owns the minimal packaging extensions needed, without
waiting for epic 18.

## P1 user story

As an integrator with no clone, I download one release artifact, verify its
checksum, and from it alone obtain the compiled scripts with their identities, the
runnable journey, and the fixtures — then reproduce the epic's claim-and-maintenance
evidence.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A uniquely versioned release is published by the **pipeline from a tag**, not
      built by hand and uploaded. A hand-built artifact attests to a provenance it
      does not have.
- [ ] The artifact carries: the compiled scripts and their **actual** identities —
      both the pinned unapplied hashes and, where applicable, the applied ones with
      their parameters; the runnable journey; the contract fixtures; and a checksum
      manifest.
- [ ] Its identities are the ones CI enforces, checked **from the downloaded
      artifact** rather than from the repository.
- [ ] **Downloaded-artifact reproduction**: a fresh extraction outside every
      worktree reproduces the epic's evidence by its own documented commands.
      Reproducing from the repository does not satisfy this row.
- [ ] Earlier runnable journeys are retained, not replaced.
- [ ] Epic 15's v0.2.0 and its simulator asset are preserved untouched.
- [ ] The release is marked as epic-scoped, so nobody mistakes it for the milestone
      or product artifact.
- [ ] The release notes state plainly what is **not** covered: recovery and
      retirement belong to epic 17, and the `LI`/`LM`/`LC` evidence is finite
      fixture execution rather than a statement about arbitrary transactions.
- [ ] Protected CI passes on the release commit.

## What must not happen

- No relabelling of a design-only archive as an on-chain release.
- No unrelated workflow, secret or branch-protection change.
- No pin, lock or compiler change to make packaging easier.
- No claim that the epic's consumer-conformance obligation is discharged: #16's
  compatibility evidence pins the accepted epic-15 release, which this release
  consumes rather than replaces.

Parent #16. Requires the row-execution slices — a release whose evidence cannot be
reproduced is the defect this row exists to prevent. Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`, asset sha256
`acbabdf54a271251bd73bf9d84ab2c901107045a7dd77d28a391f22cdd53b0e5`.

## Goal

The contract's maintenance and cancellation rows now have scripts to execute
against (#52). Every row in this epic so far has been proved at model level by
epic 15 or at Aiken level by #52 — **none of `LM` or `LC` has touched a ledger.**
This executes them.

| row | accepted | what the ledger must show |
|---|---|---|
| `LM01-maintenance-accepts` | yes | signed maintenance changes the payment destination; control, commitment and quorum survive unchanged |
| `LM02-maintenance-unauthorized-refused` | no | the same transaction without the controller signature is refused |
| `LM03-maintenance-field-tamper-refused` | no | signed, but a preserved field altered — refused |
| `LM04-maintenance-quorum-alteration-refused` | no | signed, but the retirement quorum altered — refused |
| `WR01-insert-request-refund-roundtrip` | — | the refund address recorded at request time round-trips on chain |
| `LC01-cancellation-stored-refund-accepts` | yes | cancellation paying the stored refund is accepted and the approval is consumed |
| `LC02-cancellation-redirect-refused` | no | a presented refund differing from the stored one is refused |
| `LC03-insert-attestation-cancellation-refused` | no | Insert approval alone does not authorize cancellation |
| `LC04-folded-claim-cancellation-refused` | no | a folded claim cannot be cancelled — the approval was consumed at fold |
| `LC06-cancellation-replay-refused` | no | a second cancellation against a consumed approval is refused |

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract tester, I claim a name, set and replace its payment address,
and exercise cancellation — and each refusal above is refused **by a validator on a
real devnet**, for the reason its row names.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All ten rows execute against a real devnet, each reaching the outcome its row
      specifies.
- [ ] Every refusal is asserted on its **reason**, attributable to the condition
      under test. A transaction failing on a fee, a missing input, malformed CBOR or
      any other incidental error does **not** satisfy its row and must fail the run
      — the discipline #41 established: keep the transaction well-formed, re-seal
      the script integrity hash, and let the validator be what refuses.
- [ ] `LM01` proves **preservation**, not just acceptance: control, commitment and
      quorum are read back from the chain and compared field by field against their
      pre-maintenance values, using the merged codec.
- [ ] `LC01` proves the approval is **consumed**: after cancellation the approval
      token no longer exists on chain.
- [ ] `LC04` is run **after a real fold**, so the consumed-at-fold behaviour #52
      fixed is what does the refusing — not a contrived state.
- [ ] `LC06` is run **after a successful `LC01`**, so replay is refused against a
      genuinely consumed approval.
- [ ] After the refusals, the authenticated state is read back **unchanged** — no
      rejected attempt left a trace.
- [ ] Controls: a row whose transaction is actually valid (so it succeeds) must fail
      the run, and a refusal matched against the wrong reason must fail the run.
- [ ] CI runs them.

## Why each row needs its own ledger evidence

#52's Aiken tests prove the validators refuse **given a constructed script
context**. They say nothing about whether a real transaction can be built that
presents that context, nor whether the MPFS substrate and the naming scripts
compose as the correspondence record claims. That composition is what this slice
tests, and it is where a mistaken correspondence would finally show.

Parent #16. Requires #52 (the scripts) and the merged codec. Contract epic 15
v0.2.0, commit `13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

No change to the imported MPFS partition, pins, locks or compiler. No fifth datum
field. Recovery (`LR`) and retirement (`LO`) are epic 17.

Closes #52.

The imported MPFS partition compiles `request`, `staking` and `state` and nothing
else — verified from the blueprint. The contract's maintenance and cancellation
rows name an application validator and a representative policy that did not exist,
so those rows had nothing to execute against. This writes them.

## The scripts

Their own Aiken tree with its own flake and a **copied** lock, leaving the imported
partition byte-identical (the slice gate re-checks every imported validator).

| script | purposes | params | hash |
|---|---|---|---|
| application | spend + mint | 0 | `b180c9341384072edc93d75c573d10f5f590224ff117e9de1d6a06ff` |
| representative | mint | 1 | `6f14bdea9ab880c3b6934f43942ace2b971d13a8f4123f090677f1dc` |

Pinned with parameter counts and checked in CI, the same way the imported
validators are.

## What they enforce, traced to the rows

The witness columns are the specification. `LM01` and `LM02` differ **only** in the
control signature, so maintenance requires it and its absence alone refuses.
`LM03` is signed but tampers a field; `LM04` is signed but alters the quorum.

- maintenance requires the controller signature, **preserves** control, commitment
  and quorum, and leaves the destination free;
- the datum is the **four fields** in the accepted encoding — `fifth_field_refuses`;
- cancellation compares the presented refund against the one bound into the
  withdraw approval.

59 checks, 0 errors. Negations go beyond the rows:
`destination_equal_to_control_refuses`, `maintenance_value_shrink_refuses`,
`maintenance_with_two_continuations_refuses`, `burn_unbound_name_refuses`,
`fold_altering_datum_refuses`.

## Cancellation cannot ride MPFS retract

I suggested it probably could, reading `nativeSpend` on the `LC` rows. That was
refuted with specifics: the MPFS `Request` datum has no refund field, there is no
withdraw-approval binding, and retract authenticates by owner signature while the
`LC` rows are unsigned. So the refund comparison is new script code, and the
approval is a minted attestation rather than a signature — which is what "separate
cancellation approval is required" means in practice.

## `LC04` was not enforced, and a test is what found it

The source claimed, in a comment, that fold and replay refuse "because the approval
is already consumed". No test executed either row, and my gate did not ask for them
by name — my defect.

The comment was **false**. `Fold` preserved the claim's value, so a withdraw
approval flowed into the folded record and **a folded claim could be cancelled** —
precisely what `LC04` forbids.

`Fold` now consumes the approval: burned exactly once, the record inheriting the
value minus it, which is what the policy was already documented as doing. No
redeemer changed, no test weakened. `lc04_folded_claim_cancellation_refuses` and
`lc06_cancellation_replay_refuses` hold it now.

That is the fourth comment in this epic to outrun its code, and the first where the
described behaviour was actually wrong.

## Scope

Authored and tested at Aiken level. **The `LM` and `LC` rows are not yet executed
on a ledger** — that is the next slice, and it needed these to exist. Aiken tests
are this slice's evidence, and passing tests are not a statement about arbitrary
transactions.

Closes #51.

The naming codec sat at top-level `naming/`, above `offchain/`. A flake cannot
reference paths above its own root, so `offchain/flake.nix` could not compile it —
which is why the `LI01` runner had to execute through the locked dev shell and was
the only slice in this epic outside CI.

That placement was a mistake of this epic's own making: an earlier decision put the
journey inside `offchain/` for exactly this flake-root reason, and the next piece
went to top level anyway. The compiler caught it, not review.

## The move

The naming modules are now exposed modules of the offchain library, so the `li01`
executable depends on the library instead of reaching across a path boundary.
Git records the move as pure renames:

```
{naming => offchain/naming}/src/Naming/Datum.hs          | 0
{naming => offchain/naming}/src/Naming/Request.hs        | 0
{naming => offchain/naming}/src/Naming/Wire.hs           | 0
{naming => offchain/naming}/src/Naming/Wire/Vectors.hs   | 0
{naming => offchain/naming}/test/Main.hs                 | 0
```

Zero content change on all five — verified independently against merged `main` by
hashing each file, not inferred from the rename detection. The vendored vector
bytes and their v0.2.0 provenance are untouched, and the suite still passes 17
checks over the four vectors at the new path.

## What this restores

`LI01` now runs as a packaged app with **no dev shell**, and CI gains a `li01` job
on the same convention as the journey: `needs: blueprint`, `MPFS_BLUEPRINT` from
the onchain flake, then `nix run`. The vector job is retained, repointed.

## One precise caveat about the local evidence

The local hermetic receipt used `path:` flake semantics. The reason is real: nix
omits untracked files from a git-tree flake source, the moved directory was
untracked pre-commit, and the slice fence rightly forbade staging to make the
build see it. So the receipt proves the packaged build works with the sources
present.

**CI's run on this PR is the authoritative proof of the packaged path**, because
there the sources are tracked and the invocation is the ordinary one. If that job
fails, this PR is wrong regardless of the local receipt.

Closes #47.

The accepted v0.2.0 contract specifies canonical initialization as an abstract
row — opaque identities, and an outcome that depends on which witnesses execute —
and its acceptance note leaves the concrete ledger partition to the on-chain
epics. This executes that row.

## What ran

```
[li01] li01-seed-consumed: 400 tx=3f444e1300346875d8462a4af81f16ca8fd0e26ef1d232b515b14a79a8b672cf
[li01] li01-witness-shape: seedSpend=<outRef> (script-witnessed by the applied state policy's mint branch)
[li01] li01-binding-from-chain: registry=<UTxO> validatorScript=0x874e476d…
[li01] li01-state-matches-row: consumedSeeds=[400] == result.state consumedSeeds=[400]
[li01] datum-from-chain: controlAddress=0x60f92331… paymentDestination=none nextControlCommitment=… retirementQuorum=…
```

The checkpoint datum is **decoded from what the chain holds** using the codec
proven byte-exact against the contract (#45), not compared against what was
submitted. `paymentDestination=none` exercises the option's none branch. The
applied state hash `0x874e476d…` derives from the pinned `0x64d1afbf…`, agreeing
with what #43 established independently.

The row's **absences** are asserted too: `LI01` mints no representative, and the
control proves that absence is checked (expecting quantity 1 fails against an
observed 0).

## Controls

| control | result |
|---|---|
| wrong datum field | exit 1 — expected commitment `0x46c83d16` vs decoded `0xb937c2e9` |
| wrong representative quantity | exit 1 — expected 1 vs observed 0 |
| state not matching the row | exit 1 — expected `[400,401]` vs observed `[400]` |

## Two findings from the correspondence record

It moves from intended to realised where this run exercised it, and records what
the ledger actually showed:

- **`seedSpend` is enforced by the applied state policy's mint branch**, not by a
  validator on the seed. There is no separate seed validator in the frozen
  partition; the bootstrap enforcement lives in the mint policy, whose redeemer
  requires the seed input and exactly one token named by it.
- **`representativePolicy` has no object to bind to.** The frozen partition
  compiles three validators — `request`, `staking`, `state` — and contains no
  representative minting policy and no naming application policy.

The second reorders the epic's remaining work: the claim, maintenance and
cancellation rows cannot execute against scripts that do not exist. Filed as #52,
which is now the critical path.

## One way this slice is weaker than its predecessors — stated plainly

**It is not in CI.** Every earlier slice landed with a job that re-runs its
evidence on a clean runner. This one cannot yet: the naming codec lives at
`naming/`, above `offchain/`, and a flake cannot reference paths above its own
root — so the runner cannot be a packaged app and executes through the locked dev
shell instead. The evidence here is a recorded local run, not a continuously
enforced one.

#51 relocates the codec inside the flake root and re-takes this receipt on the
hermetic path, at which point `LI01` joins the other jobs. Accepting it in this
state is a deliberate, recorded choice, not an oversight.

Executing one accepting row says nothing about arbitrary transactions.

## Goal

Realising `LI01` (#47) made the correspondence record specific enough to expose a
gap: **the on-chain scripts the remaining rows name do not exist.**

The frozen MPFS partition compiles three validators — `request`, `staking`,
`state` — verified from the blueprint. There is no representative minting policy
and no naming application policy. `LI01` worked because canonical initialization
is realisable on the MPFS substrate alone: the registry UTxO is an MPFS state
UTxO, and `seedSpend` is enforced by the state policy's mint branch.

Everything after initialization is different. A certified Insert that mints a
representative, and the maintenance and cancellation rows that spend at an
application validator, need on-chain code this repository does not have.

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract implementer, Singular's own validators exist, compile, and
have pinned script identities — so the contract's claim, maintenance and
cancellation rows have something real to execute against.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A representative minting policy and a naming application validator exist as
      Aiken source in **their own tree** with their own `aiken.toml`, built by
      their own flake. Not in `onchain/`: that tree is byte-exact custody of the
      import and its gates enforce it.
- [ ] The flake copies the existing lock rather than regenerating it, and keeps the
      inputs header verbatim — the pattern and the reason from the two-flake split.
- [ ] The validators enforce what the contract requires of them, each requirement
      traced to the row that demands it:
      - the representative is one per naming record, minted under the
        representative policy;
      - the application validator holds the **four-field** naming datum in the
        accepted encoding and nothing else;
      - control and recovery fields are preserved across ordinary maintenance
        (`LM01`), and unauthorized or field-tampering attempts fail (`LM02`,
        `LM03`, `LM04`);
      - the refund address recorded at request time is compared at cancellation
        (`WR01`, `LC01`, `LC02`).
- [ ] Their compiled hashes are pinned in the identity manifest and enforced in CI,
      the same way the imported validators are, with parameter counts recorded.
- [ ] Aiken-level tests execute each enforced condition **and its negation**: a
      validator that has never refused is an unexercised guard.
- [ ] The correspondence record's `applicationPolicy` and `representativePolicy`
      entries move from "no object to bind to" to a named script identity.

## What this issue is not

It does not execute the `LM` or `LC` rows on a ledger — that follows, once there
is something to execute against. It does not change the imported partition, the
contract, or the four-field datum.

## Honest note on scope

This is the epic's critical path, and it was not visible until `LI01` forced the
correspondence to be concrete. Any earlier statement implying the remaining rows
were a matter of wiring — including mine — was wrong.

## Dependencies

Parent #16. Follows #47 (the realised correspondence) and #51 (the codec's
relocation, so runners stay hermetic). Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

## Goal

`naming/` sits at the repository root, above `offchain/`. A flake cannot reference
paths above its own root, so `offchain/flake.nix` cannot compile the naming codec
— and any runner that needs both the codec and the transaction builder therefore
cannot be a packaged `nix run` app. The `LI01` runner (#47) had to execute through
the locked dev shell for this reason.

That is weaker than the hermetic path #31 established: a fresh runner with no dev
shell cannot run it. Every remaining functional row will want the codec **and** a
hermetic runner, so the structure should be fixed before they are built on it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The naming codec lives inside the offchain flake root (`offchain/naming/` or
      as modules of the offchain package — implementer's choice), so
      `offchain/flake.nix` can compile it.
- [ ] The naming wire-vector suite still passes **byte-exactly** against the
      vendored v0.2.0 vectors, with its provenance comments intact. The bytes do
      not change.
- [ ] Every runner that needs the codec can be invoked as a packaged app with no
      dev shell — demonstrated by running one on a clean invocation path.
- [ ] The `LI01` runner from #47 is switched to that hermetic path and its receipt
      re-taken.
- [ ] CI job names and paths updated; the vector job keeps running.
- [ ] No change to the vendored vector bytes, the pinned release, imported MPFS
      sources, pins, locks or compiler.

## Why not leave it

The dev-shell path works and is a legitimate surface here. But "works on a machine
with the dev shell" is precisely the property #31's devnet failure taught this
epic not to accept, and the cost of the move grows with every slice that imports
the codec.

## Dependencies

Parent #16. Follows #47 so its receipt is re-taken on the new path.

No behaviour change, no new dependency, no contract change.

## Goal

`LI01` proves canonical initialization can be done. The seven refusal rows prove
it cannot be done *wrongly* — and they are where the canonical binding earns its
name. Without them, an initialization path that accepts everything would pass
`LI01` and look finished.

| row | what must be refused |
|---|---|
| `LI02-alternate-seed-refused` | initializing from a seed that is not the canonical one |
| `LI03-second-seed-rival-registry-refused` | a second seed standing up a rival registry |
| `LI04-substituted-registry-refused` | a substituted registry identity |
| `LI05-substituted-policy-refused` | a substituted application policy |
| `LI06-repeated-canonical-seed-refused` | re-using the canonical seed after it was consumed |
| `LI07-substituted-representative-policy-refused` | a substituted representative policy |
| `LI08-substituted-validator-script-refused` | a substituted validator script |

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract tester, each of the seven wrong initializations is rejected
on the ledger, and I can see which binding element each attempt substituted and
why the rejection is attributable to that substitution rather than to an
unrelated error.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All seven rows execute against a real devnet and are **refused**.
- [ ] Each refusal is asserted on its **reason**, attributable to the substituted
      element. A transaction that fails on a fee, a missing input, malformed CBOR
      or any other incidental error does **not** satisfy its row, and the run must
      fail in that case — as #41 established for the cage guards.
- [ ] `LI06` specifically demonstrates the seed cannot be replayed **after a
      successful `LI01`**, so the consumed-seed state is doing the work.
- [ ] Each row names, in its output, which binding element it substituted and what
      the canonical value was.
- [ ] After the seven refusals, the canonical state is read back **unchanged** —
      no rejected attempt left a trace.
- [ ] Controls: a row whose attempt is actually canonical (so it succeeds) must
      fail the run, and a rejection matched against the wrong reason must fail the
      run.
- [ ] CI runs them.

## Why attribution is the hard part

Seven transactions that all fail is easy and worth almost nothing. The value is
in each failing *for the reason its row names*, which means each attempt must be
well-formed except for the one substitution under test — the same discipline #41
used: keep the transaction valid, re-seal the script integrity hash, and let the
validator be the thing that refuses.

## Dependencies

Parent #16, and **#47** — the realised correspondence is what these rows
substitute against. Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

## Non-goals

No change to imported MPFS sources, pins, locks or compiler. No fifth datum
field. Maintenance (`LM`) and cancellation (`LC`) are separate; recovery (`LR`)
and retirement (`LO`) are epic 17.

## Goal

The four v0.2.0 wire vectors now exist twice in the repository: vendored into
`naming/src/Naming/Wire/Vectors.hs` with their provenance, and in epic 15's
merged corpus at `lean/lifecycle-corpus.json`.

The duplication is deliberate — a consumed contract is pinned, and reading the
live file would make Singular's encoding follow whatever that file becomes. But
it leaves a blind spot: if epic 15 revises its corpus, **nothing says so**. The
vendored copy would keep passing against bytes the contract no longer ships.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A check compares the vendored vectors against the corresponding rows of the
      committed `lean/lifecycle-corpus.json` and reports any divergence,
      identifying the vector and the differing bytes.
- [ ] Divergence is **surfaced, not silently resolved**: the vendored bytes stay
      pinned to v0.2.0, and the check's job is to say that the live corpus has
      moved — a human decides whether to adopt the new contract.
- [ ] The check runs in CI.
- [ ] A bounded control demonstrates it firing: a deliberate one-byte difference
      between the two copies must be reported with both values.
- [ ] The check states which release the vendored copy is pinned to, so its output
      is readable without reading the source.

## Why this shape

Re-pointing the suite at the live corpus would be the wrong fix: it would make
the codec track an unpinned file and silently change what Singular claims to
implement. The point is to keep the pin and make drift visible.

Parent #16. Builds on #45.

No change to the vendored bytes, to the pinned release, or to epic 15's corpus.
