Closes #45.

Before anything puts a Singular naming datum on a chain, the encoding has to be
**the contract's** encoding. Epic 15's accepted v0.2.0 ships four byte-exact wire
vectors for exactly that, negatives included.

## What the suite asserts

| vector | assertion | result |
|---|---|---|
| `WD01-four-field-roundtrip` | `encode(fixture)` equals `expectedBytes` **byte for byte** (205 bytes); decode reproduces the recorded structure; re-encode reproduces the bytes | pass |
| `WD01` negative | `malformedBytes` decodes to **nothing**, matching `malformedResult: null` | pass |
| `WD02-datum-hash-refused` | an attached datum hash instead of an inline datum is refused | pass |
| `WD03-two-destinations-refused` | two payment destinations are refused | pass |
| `WR01-insert-request-refund-roundtrip` | the refund address round-trips (36-byte commitment); a redirected refund decodes but compares **unequal**, reproducing `{accepted:false, reason:"withdraw-refund-address"}` | pass |

17 checks, all green. Byte equality, not structural similarity: an encoder
producing a different serialisation that "means the same thing" would be wrong
here, and the contract right.

The datum is **four fields** — `controlAddress`, `paymentDestination` as the
option, `nextControlCommitment` digest, `retirementQuorum`. There is no fifth.

## The suite was observed failing

| control | result |
|---|---|
| one byte of encoder output changed | 4/17 checks fail, naming byte index 1: got `0x7a`, expected `0x79` |
| decoder swaps two quorum members | 2/17 fail on the decoded comparison |
| parser accepts truncated input | 2/17 fail — both malformed negatives flipped positive |

The third is the one that matters: it is the mutation that would otherwise leave
a codec looking correct while accepting garbage.

## Provenance

The vectors are vendored into `naming/src/Naming/Wire/Vectors.hs` with the
release commit `13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d` and asset sha256
`acbabdf54a271251bd73bf9d84ab2c901107045a7dd77d28a391f22cdd53b0e5` recorded in
the source, so CI needs no network and a reader can tell which contract the codec
agrees with.

Epic 15's corpus is also on `main` at `lean/lifecycle-corpus.json`, so these bytes
now exist twice. That is deliberate — a consumed contract is pinned, and reading
the live file would make Singular's encoding follow whatever that file becomes.
The cost is that drift between the two is invisible; a cross-check is filed as
follow-up rather than added after the gate passed.

## The correspondence record

`offchain/naming-correspondence.md` maps each abstract identity in the contract's
`LI` rows (`registry`, `applicationPolicy`, `representativePolicy`,
`validatorScript`, `canonicalSeed`) and each `executingWitness` flag to the
concrete ledger object intended to realise it.

**Every entry is marked intended-but-unproven.** v0.2.0's own acceptance note
states the concrete ledger witness and script partition remains abstract and is
implementation work for the on-chain epics, so this mapping is epic 16's design,
not something the contract blessed. #47 is where it becomes realised.

Finite vector execution is not a universal decoder theorem.

## Goal

With the naming datum codec proven against the contract's own bytes (#45), put
`LI01-canonical-initialization-accepts` on a real ledger.

The contract's `LI01` row is abstract: identities are opaque integers and the
outcome depends on which witnesses execute (`seedSpend: true`, everything else
false, no required signers). v0.2.0's acceptance note states the concrete ledger
witness and script partition is this epic's work. #45 writes down the intended
correspondence; this issue makes it real and runs the row.

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract tester, I initialize a Singular registry by consuming the
canonical seed, and the state the chain then holds carries the exact
representative and the four-field checkpoint the contract's `LI01` row
prescribes — decoded from the chain, not assumed from what I submitted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `LI01` executes as a real transaction on a devnet: the canonical seed UTxO
      is consumed, and the row's `executingWitness` shape is honoured —
      `seedSpend` present; `applicationMint`, `applicationSpend`,
      `representativeMint`, `authenticatedRead`, `nativeSpend` absent; no
      required signers and no quorum signers.
- [ ] The resulting state is read back and compared against the row's
      `result.state` (`consumedSeeds: [<canonical seed>]`), by reading the chain.
- [ ] The initial checkpoint datum is **decoded from what the chain holds** using
      the #45 codec and equals the prescribed four fields. Trusting the submitted
      value does not satisfy this row.
- [ ] The row's witness shape is asserted as the contract states it, **including
      what must not happen**: `seedSpend` present; `applicationMint`,
      `applicationSpend`, `representativeMint`, `authenticatedRead` and
      `nativeSpend` absent; no required signers and no quorum signers. `LI01`
      mints no representative — that belongs to the claim rows, not to
      initialization.
- [ ] The applied script identities used are derived from the pinned unapplied
      ones and named, per the existing `derived-applied-identity` check.
- [ ] The correspondence record from #45 is updated from *intended* to *realised*,
      naming the concrete object each abstract identity became in this run.
- [ ] Bounded controls demonstrate the row's checks failing: a wrong datum field,
      a wrong representative quantity, and a read-back that does not match
      `result.state` must each fail the run naming the mismatch.
- [ ] CI runs it.

## Scope

One accepting row. `LI02`–`LI08` are refusals and are filed separately;
maintenance (`LM`) and cancellation (`LC`) likewise. Recovery (`LR`) and
retirement (`LO`) are epic 17.

Executing one accepting row is not a statement about arbitrary transactions.

## Dependencies

Parent #16, and **#45** — the codec must be proven against the published bytes
before the datum this row writes can be trusted. Contract epic 15 v0.2.0, commit
`13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`.

## Non-goals

No change to imported MPFS sources, pins, locks or compiler. No fifth datum
field. No naming behaviour beyond this row.


## Correction (2026-09-10)

An earlier version of this issue required the representative to be minted and
asserted. That was wrong: `LI01`'s `executingWitness` sets `representativeMint:
false`, along with `applicationMint`, `applicationSpend`, `authenticatedRead` and
`nativeSpend`. Canonical initialization consumes the canonical seed and
establishes the canonical binding; the representative mint belongs to the claim
rows. The criterion above now asserts the row's witness shape, including the
absences, instead of demanding a mint the contract does not prescribe.

Before anything puts a Singular naming datum on a chain, the encoding has to be

vectors for exactly this, and they include negative cases:

| vector | what it fixes |
|---|---|
| `WD01-four-field-roundtrip` | the canonical four-field datum, with `expectedBytes`, `shape {arity:4, innerIndex:0, outerIndex:0}`, and `malformedBytes` that must decode to nothing |
| `WD02-datum-hash-refused` | an attached datum hash instead of an inline datum is refused |
| `WD03-two-destinations-refused` | two payment destinations are refused |
| `WR01-insert-request-refund-roundtrip` | the refund address round-trips in the request, and a redirected refund compares unequal to the stored one |

This issue implements the codec and proves it against those bytes. It also
produces the **correspondence record**, because the codec is the first place the
abstract contract meets concrete ledger objects and the mapping should be written
down where it is first needed rather than later.

`LI01` on a real ledger is filed separately: a codec proven against published
bytes is a prerequisite for it, and is worth reviewing on its own.

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract implementer, I encode and decode the four-field naming datum
and get byte-for-byte agreement with the accepted contract's vectors — and the
malformed, datum-hash and two-destination cases are refused, not quietly
accepted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A naming datum codec encodes the four fields — `controlAddress`,
      `paymentDestination` as the option (`constr(0,[])` / `constr(1,[bytes])`),
      `nextControlCommitment` digest, `retirementQuorum` — and decodes them back.
      **No fifth field.**
- [ ] `WD01`: encoding the fixture produces `expectedBytes` **exactly**; decoding
      `expectedBytes` produces the recorded `decoded` structure; re-encoding
      reproduces the same bytes. Byte equality, not structural similarity.
- [ ] `WD01` negative: `malformedBytes` decodes to **nothing**, matching
      `malformedResult: null`.
- [ ] `WD02` and `WD03` are refused as the vectors record.
- [ ] `WR01`: the refund address round-trips through the request encoding, and
      the redirected refund compares **unequal** to the stored one, matching the
      vector's `comparisonResult`.

Closes #43.

Watching the chain refuse transactions in #41 showed that the script hashes the
node names are **not** the ones `onchain/script-identity.json` pins: `request`
takes 2 parameters and `state` takes 1, so the scripts that actually run have
different hashes. `staking` takes none and coincides.

must not move when a dependency or the compiler changes. But it is not the
identity a transaction carries, and nothing said so.

## The chain is now derived and checked, not assumed

```
derived-applied-identity: state applied 0x874e476d… = unapplied 0x64d1afbf…
  with parameters previousPolicies=[] (1 parameter) — the boot tx carried exactly this script
derived-applied-identity: request applied 0x8c7f99ec… = unapplied 0x6b5ce701…
  with parameters statePolicyId=0x874e476d… cageToken=0xc1f1c9b0… (2 parameters)
  — the update tx carried exactly this script
derived-applied-identity: staking 0x4ab26c95… takes no parameters (0)
  — applied and unapplied coincide, matching the pin
```

Each applied hash is computed by applying this instance's parameters to the
pinned unapplied script and then required to equal the script the transaction
actually carried. A wrong parameter or a wrong expected hash fails the run naming
both values — both demonstrated.

Each validator entry now records its parameter count, so the manifest itself says
which entries are parameter-dependent. **No pinned hash value changed.**

instance is a devnet cage is cheaper than discovering the ambiguity inside a

body:
Closes #41.

Everything this epic had merged exercised the happy path. No validator in these
trees had ever been observed *rejecting* anything — and a guard that has never
refused might be permissive, mis-wired, or checking the wrong field, while every
green run looked identical.

## The three refusals

| case | mutation | validator that must refuse |
|---|---|---|
| `reject-forged-identity` | `Contribute` redeemer names a state UTxO carrying no state token | `request.request.spend` |
| `reject-tampered-output` | certified output keeps the `StateDatum` shape, root replaced by its byte complement | `state.state.spend` |
| `reject-missing-witness` | required signer dropped from the body, fee-payer witness kept so phase 1 passes | `state.state.spend` |

Each mutation keeps the transaction well-formed and **re-seals the script
integrity hash**, so the refusal comes from phase-2 validation rather than a
structural error. A rejection for the wrong reason fails the run; so does a
negative case that succeeds.

Each case asserts the validator script hash the node names, **derived from the
config** rather than hard-coded, so it tracks the parameters instead of today's
values.

## The positive control

After the three refusals the authenticated state is read back unchanged —
`root=0x7b43b759…`, `request_utxos=1`, no trace. Without it, "rejected" could
mean "partially applied".

## The harness was observed failing

| control | result |
|---|---|
| a negative case made valid | exit 1 — the guard did not refuse, named |
| a rejection matched against a phase-1 reason | exit 1 — naming what actually came back |

## Scope

These are **MPFS cage** guards. Singular's naming negative cases — duplicate
claims, representative forgery — cannot exist until the naming layer does, and
nothing here suggests otherwise.

Noted while doing this, and filed separately: the hashes the node names are the
parameter-**applied** script hashes, whereas `onchain/script-identity.json` pins

two layers differ; `staking` takes none and coincides. The manifest pins the

identity a transaction carries.

## Goal

#16 requires that negative cases reject forged identities, changed certified
outputs and missing executing witnesses. Everything merged so far exercises the
**happy path**: the journey boots, inserts, applies and verifies, and the devnet
suite covers upstream's own scenarios. Nothing in this epic has yet watched the
on-chain validators *refuse* a transaction.

A validator that has never been observed rejecting anything is an unexercised
guard. Make the journey submit transactions that must fail, and require them to
fail for the stated reason.

## P1 user story

As an integrator, the journey shows me that the on-chain validators reject a
forged policy identity, a tampered certified output and a missing required
witness — and if any of those were accepted, the command would fail.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At least three negative transactions are submitted to a real devnet in the
      same run, each expected to be **rejected by the on-chain validator**:
      a forged policy or state-token identity; a tampered certified output
      (correct shape, wrong content); and a transaction missing a required
      executing witness.
- [ ] Each rejection is asserted on its **reason**, not merely on failure. A
      transaction that fails for the wrong reason — a malformed CBOR, a fee
      error, a missing input — does not prove the validator rejected it, and the
      run must fail in that case.
- [ ] If any negative transaction is **accepted**, the run fails loudly and names
      which guard did not hold.
- [ ] The run also proves the positive control: after the negative cases, the
      authenticated state is unchanged — a rejected transaction left no trace.
- [ ] Bounded controls demonstrate the harness failing: a negative case whose
      transaction is actually valid (so it succeeds) must fail the run, and a
      rejection matched against the wrong reason must fail the run.
- [ ] CI runs it.

The guards being exercised belong to the imported MPFS validators, which the
Singular naming application will sit on top of. Proving they reject forged
identities now means the naming layer inherits a harness that has been observed
working, rather than one written at the same time as the behaviour it checks.

body:
Closes #39.

The journey runner narrated a state transition and verified nothing. If the
proof machinery were broken it would have printed the same green line.

## What it now proves

```
[journey] verify-absent: proved absent key=hello against chain root 0x0000…
[journey] verify-present: proved present key=hello value=world root=0x7b43b759…
[journey] verify-false-claim: rejected false claim key=hello claimed value=forged:
          proof implies root 0x5f27b859… which differs from the chain read root 0x7b43b759…
```

Each verification recomputes the root a proof implies and compares it to **the
root read back from the chain** — never a root the runner computed itself. A
proof checked against its own source proves only that the code agrees with
itself, which is the failure this slice removes.

Any failing verification exits non-zero naming the key, the expected root and
the computed one.

## The checks were observed failing

| control | result |
|---|---|
| absence asserted for a key that is present | exit 1 — "the state holds it" |
| presence asserted with a wrong value | exit 1 — proof implies `0x63b5b3…`, chain read `0x7b43b759…` |
| the false claim made true | exit 1 — "the negative case is not negative" |

The third matters most: the negative case is exercised every run, and if it ever
succeeds the run fails. That is what stops it rotting into decoration.

## Scope

This verifies the **MPFS cage substrate's** authenticated state. It is not
Singular's naming claim — no naming-claim behaviour exists yet. The naming layer
inherits this machinery when it arrives, which is why it is worth having now.

No validator, pin, lock, compiler or `script-identity.json` change; all 23
imported Haskell sources remain byte-identical to upstream, verified by the
slice gate. The one dependency used, `mts:mpf-write`, was already a build-depends
of the library and is pinned by SHA in `cabal.project`.

## Goal

#16 requires that authenticated-state verification distinguish **absence**,
**live state**, and **non-live state**. The journey artifact from #37 currently
narrates a state transition — it reports the trie root moving — but it never
*verifies* anything: it takes the node's word for the result and would print the
same happy path if the proof machinery were broken.

Make the journey check what it claims, using the authenticated-state proofs the
imported library already provides (`Cardano.MPFS.Cage.Proof`).

## P1 user story

As an integrator, the journey tells me the key was provably absent before the
insert and provably present with the expected value after — and if either claim
were false the command would fail instead of printing a green line.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Before the insert, the runner verifies and reports that the key is
      **absent** from the authenticated state, against the root it just read.
- [ ] After the apply, it verifies and reports that the key is **present with
      the expected value**, against the new root.

      proof asserting a key or value that the state does not hold — is rejected.
      A run in which the negative case is not exercised fails.

      against a value the runner computed and kept. Verifying a claim against

For an on-chain contract the compiled script hash **is** the contract's
identity. Until now nothing enforced ours. Three hashes were known to be right
by experiment — the same values come out of `onchain/`, out of upstream's frozen
revision built with its own unmodified flake, and out of a real Aiken `v1.1.16`
binary — but that was an argument, not a check.

## What lands

- `onchain/script-identity.json` — every validator in the blueprint with its
  compiled hash, plus the upstream source revision
  `34a5bfbb8cca2cb1911b7060d0e61db28ba21e83` and the compiler that produced them
  (`v1.1.21+unknown`). Generated from a real build, never typed.
- `checks.script-identity` in the Aiken flake — compares the built blueprint
  against the manifest **in both directions over the whole validator set**, so a
  validator added or removed fails rather than passing quietly.
- `just script-identity` and a regeneration recipe: a deliberate identity change
  is made by regenerating, and the manifest diff is what a reviewer reads.
- A `script-identity` job in `.github/workflows/mpfs.yml`, on the existing
  triggers and conventions, with no new secret.

## Pinned identity

| validator | hash |
|---|---|
| `request.request.{spend,else}` | `6b5ce70130332cee6fb016866d2a03c497d313e5df62a22e12af3e5f` |
| `staking.staking.{withdraw,else}` | `4ab26c95029067185f709d140300cccb15b0b20bbd62a7e9aa2e2e10` |
| `state.state.{mint,spend,else}` | `64d1afbfe585b496a325ecacf2600210ff773368010bbab96e5cf1ce` |

## The check was observed failing

| control | result |
|---|---|
| changed hash in the manifest | fails, naming the validator, expected vs actual |
| validator deleted from the manifest | fails — built validator unrecorded |
| bogus validator added to the manifest | fails — manifest entry with no counterpart in the build |

No validator source, dependency pin, lock or compiler changed. This records the
identity that exists today and makes any future move visible; it does not decide
which compiler to pin long-term.

## Goal

Make the imported MPFS trees build where they now live. `onchain/` and
`offchain/` are byte-exact copies of
`cardano-foundation/cardano-mpfs-onchain@34a5bfbb8cca2cb1911b7060d0e61db28ba21e83`
taken by #19, which deliberately compiled nothing and repaired nothing. Eight
relative paths that the directory placement broke are recorded in
`PROVENANCE.md`. This slice repairs exactly those, inside the imported trees,
and proves the result by running the upstream builds.

Compilation belongs here, not retrospectively to #19. The custody commit is
preserved unchanged as the first commit of this slice's branch.

## P1 user story

As a Singular developer, I run one command in `onchain/` and get the MPFS
Plutus blueprint, and one command in `offchain/` and get the Haskell cage
package built — from the imported sources, with the imported dependency pins
unchanged.

## Architectural decision (owner-bound, not for the implementer to revisit)

The upstream root `flake.nix` spanned both trees (`src = cleanSource ./.` plus
`import ./haskell/nix/{project,checks,apps}.nix`). That shape cannot survive
the split: a flake may not reference paths above its own root, and Singular's
repository root already has its own `flake.nix` that this epic may not touch
without milestone arbitration.

Therefore: **two self-contained flakes**, `onchain/flake.nix` (Aiken) and
`offchain/flake.nix` (Haskell), each rooted in the tree it builds.

- Dependency pins are **preserved, never regenerated**. The imported root
  `flake.lock` supplies the pinned inputs; a lock is copied, not recomputed,
  and `nix flake update` is forbidden.
- `aiken.lock`, `aiken.toml` and `cabal.project` keep their exact imported
  bytes. No `index-state` change, no `--sha256` change, no dependency upgrade,
  no `allow-newer` addition.
- No Singular root file changes: not `/flake.nix`, `/flake.lock`, `/justfile`,
  `/nix/**`, `/lean/**`, `/simulator/**`, `/docs/**`, `/specs/**`. If the slice
  appears to need one, it stops and returns the reason.
- No factoring, no shared-library extraction, no deduplication between the two
  trees, no submodule, no symlink into any checkout.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the eight recorded breaks is either repaired inside the imported
      trees or explicitly returned as out of scope with its reason. The
      repaired path is named against its `PROVENANCE.md` row.
- [ ] `aiken build` and `aiken check` succeed for `onchain/`, producing the
      blueprint, through the flake — with the Aiken compiler version and the
      three prelude dependencies exactly as `aiken.toml` and `aiken.lock` pin
      them.
- [ ] The Haskell cage package in `offchain/` builds through its flake with the
      imported `cabal.project` pins unchanged, and its unit test suite runs.
- [ ] The vector-freshness relationship between the two trees
      (`offchain` generates `validators/cage_vectors.ak`, `onchain` consumes it)
      is either re-established across the new boundary or recorded as deferred
      with the exact reason; committed vectors are not silently allowed to drift.
- [ ] The devnet E2E suite is either executed and its result reported, or
      returned with the concrete blocker (it drives a real `cardano-node`
      subprocess and may exceed this slice's budget). No E2E claim without a run.
- [ ] `git diff` against the custody commit touches only `onchain/**`,
      `offchain/**` and this slice's own records. The custody commit
      `34d7abec6ee4830e17a725fa84239af46c3ee206` is the branch's first commit,
      unchanged.
- [ ] Every build claim carries the command, its exit status and where it ran.
      A green claim without a run does not close a row.

Reproducing the upstream MPFS builds is **bootstrap evidence**. It is not
completion of #16, and it is not evidence that Singular's naming validators
exist: no claim/maintenance behavior is implemented here. Finite build success
says nothing about ledger correctness over arbitrary transactions.

Parent #16. Consumes **no** epic #15 contract, so it runs in parallel with #15.
#16's final compatibility and release evidence still pins the accepted #15
release; that dependency is unchanged and is not discharged here. Withdrawal
economics remain unanswered upstream and are not invented here.

Flat epic-owner supervision, as for #19: the owner holds the contract, decides
architecture, freezes the gates and reviews their ability to fail; GLM and Muse
do the bounded mechanical work. No auditor seat, no extra management layer.
Shared root Nix, build and docs-publication edits go to milestone arbitration
rather than being made here.

## Goal

Deliver reproducible on-chain Singular artifacts and independently establish readiness for the exact cardano-keri consumer contract, alongside the bounded naming demonstration.

## P1 user story

As a cardano-keri integrator, I obtain the versioned Singular on-chain artifacts and replay the agreed consumer transactions, observing documented conformance and explicit measured limits.

## Architectural invariants

- Consumer readiness requires exact contract-bound on-chain execution; naming success and browser/model simulation alone cannot establish it.
- Test-only fixtures/harnesses exercise scripts and ledger transaction shapes without adopting a production SDK, indexer, backend, wallet integration, resolver or UI.
- Independent acceptance is separate from author-green checks, closed issues and formal-model claims.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every agreed consumer-contract row maps to exact script/policy/schema versions and executable accepted/rejected transaction cases; uncovered or unresolved requirements remain blockers, including generic operations not exercised by naming.
- [ ] An independently reviewed conformance report binds artifact hashes, commands, inputs, observed results and limits to the exact release candidate, with no downstream implementation or full KERI protocol work inferred.
- [ ] Reproducible install/obtain/run instructions work from a clean supported environment for compiled on-chain artifacts and tests; CI checks match the release artifact and an actual usable on-chain release path exists.
- [ ] The naming claim/address/recovery/owner-or-quorum-retirement sequence is demonstrated with real on-chain execution, with pending versus Over and negative controls visible; illustrative simulator/docs state their limits.
- [ ] Execution/resource limits and unsupported environments are measured and documented; milestone acceptance distinguishes implementation, proof, independent verification and release evidence. No production/public-network readiness is claimed.

## Runnable artifact and release path

Deliver the integrated M1 versioned on-chain script/contract package and replayable consumer/naming conformance suite, with checksums, reproducibility instructions and CI/release receipts. Establish on-chain packaging from the existing documentation release foundation; current documentation publication is not an on-chain release. Graduating the temporary M1 artifact into the product release requires independent acceptance, not merely completion of this planning epic map.

## Epic release: Independently accepted consumer-conformance release

A cardano-keri integrator obtains the release and reproduces the exact agreed consumer transaction shapes and rejection cases, plus the complete bounded naming contract demonstration, from its published commands and artifacts.

This epic closes with the consolidated, installable on-chain release with exact cardano-keri consumer-contract bindings, reproducible conformance fixtures, the bounded naming journey, measured limits and independent outcome-review evidence. It integrates the accepted release from #17 and the preserved contract/claim releases from #15/#16; earlier epics must already have delivered their own releases. This release adds end-to-end on-chain consumer conformance and independent milestone outcome acceptance to the already runnable earlier releases. It cannot substitute a browser model or naming-only demo for consumer evidence. Milestone closure remains a separate owner decision based on this outcome evidence.

Its epic owner must decompose vertically: each eventual child extends this same runnable artifact with an observable behavior and the required transaction fixtures, checks and documentation. - [ ] Independent review accepts the epic's declared boundary and correspondence/compatibility evidence; limits and unverified layers are explicit.

Blocked by #17 and transitively #15/#16. Consumer contract agreement is an explicit prerequisite; off-chain scope requires later discussion and MPFS factoring remains only a possible M2.

M1: On-chain Singular support for cardano-keri. Singular's on-chain registry, policies and application-facing contracts must be sufficient for the exact agreed cardano-keri consumer contract. Existing operator-owned #10 is foundational generic-model proof work. Preserve its ownership and scope; its issue state is not independent audit acceptance. The generic model includes Delete; the naming restriction must not remove behavior required by the consumer.

Implementation child tickets remain for later epic-owner decomposition. Experiment #14 is deferred outside M1 and is not a prerequisite. A subsequently commissioned epic owner must first settle the named decisions, then decompose runnable vertical slices in dependency order and use resolve-ticket for each issue-backed PR with independent verification. No public-network/mainnet launch, bonds/prices/expiry, marketplace, transferable-name support, quorum rotation, takeover/Close or naming Delete/reuse. No claim of fee-free/deposit-free operation. Off-chain product decisions and MPFS extraction remain outside this epic.


Consumer conformance must include the actual Haskell serialization/transaction boundary, with matching datum/redeemer/parameter encoding and compiled execution evidence. Experiment #14 is deferred outside M1 and does not gate consumer acceptance; implementation language remains undecided, and a same-Scala-stack emulator or source-language-independent Plutus output alone does not establish application compatibility.


---

authority covers planning metadata only: no release tag, implementation or execution is
commissioned"* and *"Implementation child tickets remain for later epic-owner decomposition"* —
and nothing else. Every acceptance criterion, invariant, non-goal and scope fence above stands
unchanged and is not weakened by this commission.

acceptance is owned by epic 16 and is consumed, not re-derived, here.

commit `14a64a4681d3e429fab5877062b5c476c2a4bfe2`, documents `docs/design/registry-as-mpfs.md`
(the registry cardano-keri would consume, its rulings and theorems R1–R14) and
`docs/user/consumer-checklist.md` (the treasury's six-point fail-closed rule).

**The denominator is 40 rows**, derived from that contract, the v0.2.0 protocol specification and
the epic-16 implementation, in five groups: canonical identity authentication (5), generic
operations beyond naming (19), the Haskell serialization and transaction-construction boundary (8),
the consumer's own fail-closed resolution (5, with the checkpoint machine's own four checks recorded

expected to be **gaps** in the imported partition (empty fold, surplus actions, owner pinning,
refund routing), which will be reported as conformance findings with the observation that proves
them rather than omitted or asserted passing.

**Correction carried from epic 16 (LI03).** A permissionless ledger cannot prohibit a rival
registry existing. Canonical identity is established by the consumer authenticating the canonical
seed/name binding — the registry token name is SHA-256 of the canonical seed's outRef — not by a
global ledger refusal. No row here fakes that refusal or relabels an accepted rival.

**Decomposition.** Vertical children, each extending the same runnable conformance artifact under
`conformance/` with executed rows, fixtures, negative controls that are required to fail, and usable
instructions. Recovery and retirement rows (LR/LT) belong to #17; this epic's acceptance consumes
#17's exact accepted release and declares none of its rows passed.

- [ ] Complete #87: validate every applicable M1 invariant against the exact production-built Aiken UPLC using the pinned Blaster/CEK toolchain, preserving the accepted Lean clauses and readable Given/When/Then correspondence.

Missing, unsupported, unknown, stale or failing results remain blocking debt. Model-only proofs and finite executions do not establish quantified compiled-code claims.
- [ ] Enforce this separate per-obligation debt in #80 strict M1 completion and integrated publication. It supplements the existing two implementation layers; no M1 closure or integrated M1 release until all required obligations are discharged. Epic18 owns verification/gate integration; epic17 supplies repaired artifacts and implementation fixes. Existing no-extra-auditor staffing remains in force.

Full acceptance contract: https://github.com/lambdasistemi/singular/issues/87.

## Goal

Demonstrate on-chain recovery and irreversible retirement through the naming contract while implementing the relevant shared Singular custody/completion obligations.

## P1 user story

As a name controller, I recover with the committed next control key or retire through current-owner or fixed-quorum authorization, and observe that a completed retired name never resolves or becomes registrable again.

## Architectural invariants

- Control is a current key-controlled address plus a hash commitment to the next address. Recovery reveals that address, requires its payment key, preserves the NFT and installs a fresh next commitment; the old controller need not sign.
- Retirement is authorized by the current application controller OR a fixed-at-registration threshold quorum, never both and never silently next-key-only. Quorum powers exclude takeover and payment redirection.
- Retirement transfers the representative into a completion-only request; no withdrawal or escape is permitted. A later fold burns it and records permanent Over. Output creation alone executes no receiving script.
- Pending retirement is distinct from completed Over and neither yields a live naming resolution. Naming Delete/release/reuse is excluded while generic consumer behavior is preserved.

- [ ] Executable ledger cases recover after loss of the everyday key using the committed next payment key without old-controller signature, preserving NFT and installing a fresh commitment.
- [ ] Wrong recovery key/commitment, replay, unauthorized field changes and quorum-only redirection fail for the intended reasons.
- [ ] Separate positive cases retire with the current controller alone and with the fixed threshold quorum alone; insufficient quorum fails. Exact quorum members and threshold are bound at registration.
- [ ] Ledger evidence observes request custody, pending non-live resolution, irreversible completion, NFT burn and terminal Over; withdrawal, custody escape, name release/reuse and re-registration after Over fail.

## Goal

Implement Singular initialization, certified Insert, permissionless folding, authenticated application state and pending-Insert withdrawal under the frozen concrete and consumer contracts.

## P1 user story

As a naming-contract tester, I claim alice on the ledger and set, replace or clear its optional payment address, observing unique authenticated state and rejection of duplicate or unauthorized transitions.

## Architectural invariants

- Insert mints exactly the prescribed representative into the certified initial application output; the key must be absent when folded. Approval does not reserve it.
- The checkpoint contains zero or one payment destination, separate from control credentials. Ordinary address changes preserve control/recovery fields and do not mutate the registry.
- Withdrawal applies only to an unfulfilled Insert and requires distinct exact-request authorization with settled refund terms; Insert approval alone is insufficient.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Executable ledger/script cases verify canonical bootstrap, certified Insert, permissionless fold and exact NFT/initial datum/destination/value effects against the frozen contract.
- [ ] Negative cases reject duplicate claims, forged policy/registry/representative identities, changed certified outputs and missing executing witnesses.
- [ ] Authorized withdrawal of an unfulfilled Insert produces the agreed refund and token disposal with no registry transition or representative mint; unauthorized cancellation and altered refund fail.
- [ ] Authenticated-state verification distinguishes absence, live representative/application state and non-live states; set/replace/clear preserve NFT and control/recovery fields, and unauthorized changes fail.
- [ ] Cases trace each implemented shared behavior to the consumer contract and concrete model; finite fixture evidence is not represented as a proof of arbitrary transactions.

## Runnable artifact and release path

Deliver compiled on-chain registry/policy/application artifacts plus reproducible test-only transaction construction and execution fixtures for the claim/maintain vertical flow. This is verification support, not an adopted SDK/resolver/wallet product. Pin actual commands once the toolchain is selected. Package the scripts, contract versions and replayable tests into the M1 on-chain release artifact; extend the currently documentation-only publication path before this artifact can be accepted as releasable.

## Epic release: Claim and maintenance on-chain release

An integrator obtains this release and runs the bounded claim/maintenance journey: claim an absent name, reject a duplicate, observe the exact NFT/checkpoint, maintain its optional destination and exercise the settled withdrawal/refund behavior.

This epic closes with a versioned on-chain script/policy and contract bundle with test-only transaction construction and replay support for certified claim, permissionless fold, authenticated application state, authorized unfulfilled Insert withdrawal and optional address set/replace/clear. It extends the accepted executable contract/scenario release from #15 and carries its contract version and compatibility evidence. This release must be runnable and independently verifiable without waiting for recovery/retirement or final milestone assembly. Consumer ABI compatibility required for these operations and negative cases is checked here; final full consumer acceptance remains the later release.

Its epic owner must decompose vertically: each eventual child extends this same runnable artifact with an observable behavior and the required transaction fixtures, checks and documentation. A library-only layer with no runnable entry point does not finish a vertical slice. Packaging and the usable CI/release path belong to this epic; they cannot all be deferred to #18. Technical commands, version identifiers and distribution format are bound when commissioning, not invented by this metadata plan.

Release acceptance for this epic:

- [ ] A uniquely versioned, retrievable release artifact and its exact source/script/contract identities are published with install/run/replay instructions.
- [ ] The epic's complete user journey and attributable positive/negative checks reproduce from that artifact through its usable CI/release path.
- [ ] Independent review accepts the epic's declared boundary and correspondence/compatibility evidence; limits and unverified layers are explicit.
- [ ] The successor epic consumes this exact accepted release (or a recorded compatible successor), preserving prior runnable journeys.

Execution of this epic is commissioned as of 2026-09-10 under an epic owner. No final release tag is cut until a concrete complete release is reviewed through the milestone path. Every release remains on-chain or contract verification scope; no production SDK, backend, resolver, wallet integration or off-chain product is adopted.

## Dependencies and design prerequisites

Canonical initialization, script bindings, encodings, consumer shapes and withdrawal refund decisions must be stable and proved before the functional ledger implementation of this epic. That dependency on #15 is unchanged for implementation and for this epic's final compatibility and release evidence, which pins the actual accepted #15 release rather than a current fixture.

By operator ruling 2026-09-10 the epic starts in parallel with #15 on work that consumes no #15 contract: child #19, source and lock custody, begins immediately. Functional slices that depend on a #15 contract remain parked until that contract is accepted and published; #15's unfinished contracts are not assumed accepted.

## Milestone and scope

M1: On-chain Singular support for cardano-keri. Singular's on-chain registry, policies and application-facing contracts must be sufficient for the exact agreed cardano-keri consumer contract. The naming lifecycle is a bounded demonstration/test application, not evidence by itself of consumer readiness.

Off-chain scope is limited to transaction-building and devnet verification support from the MPFS on-chain repository. The indexer and separate off-chain service repository are excluded; no production SDK, wallet integration, resolver service, backend or user-facing application is promised. Transaction fixtures/harnesses are test-only verification support. MPFS common-code factoring is a possible M2, not an M1 prerequisite or commissioned extraction.

## Foundation

Existing operator-owned #10 is foundational generic-model proof work. Preserve its ownership and scope; its issue state is not independent audit acceptance. New concrete-ledger, consumer-interface and naming-application models/theorems are distinct extensions and require coordination before changes to the existing model. The generic model includes Delete; the naming restriction must not remove behavior required by the consumer.

## Child decomposition and parallelization

First child: #19 — Copy MPFS source and locks into onchain/ and offchain/. After the accepted #15 release, copy the validators and existing Haskell transaction-building/devnet support from cardano-foundation/cardano-mpfs-onchain. Preserve existing locks unchanged; no compilation, test execution, factoring, dependency upgrades or path repair in #19. Later children adapt and test that code for the ledger journey. Child #19 is the explicit operator-authorized source-and-lock custody exception: it runs now under flat epic-owner supervision with a reviewed file-identity gate, no separate ticket-owner layer and no auditor seat. Functional parallel implementation still requires stable proved contracts and explicit disjoint ownership; shared contract changes force serialization and replanning. Integrate accepted child artifacts serially into the milestone's on-chain artifact.

## Non-goals

No full KERI protocol implementation inside Singular or speculative downstream implementation. No public-network/mainnet launch, bonds/prices/expiry, marketplace, transferable-name support, quorum rotation, takeover/Close or naming Delete/reuse. No claim of fee-free/deposit-free operation. Off-chain product decisions and MPFS extraction remain outside this epic.



## Progress (2026-09-10)

Merged, with CI enforcing each: #19 MPFS source and lock custody; #31 two
self-contained flakes with builds and a hermetic devnet gate; #34 compiled script
identity pinned and enforced; #37 the epic's runnable artifact; #39 that artifact
verifying absence, presence and a rejected false claim against chain-read roots.

From `main` a person can run `nix build .#plutus-blueprint` in `onchain/`, and
`just vectors-check`, `just e2e` and `nix run .#journey` in `offchain/`. CI runs
all of them on every change to the imported trees.

Script identity is recorded and enforced: `onchain/script-identity.json` pins the
validator hashes, and a CI job fails any change that moves one. Building the
imported sources with the declared Aiken `v1.1.16` produces the same hashes as
the pinned `v1.1.21`, so the inherited compiler discrepancy is recorded and does
not affect contract identity.

**Not yet implemented**, and gated outside this epic: the functional naming
slices, which this issue binds to the frozen contract from #15 (its #21, #24, #25
are open); settled pending-Insert withdrawal and refund, which needs the
unanswered decision on who authorizes withdrawal and who receives the locked
funds; and the versioned on-chain release, pending a ruling on whether this epic
ships through #15's release staging tooling or builds its own path.

Everything delivered so far is bootstrap and verification support for the MPFS
cage substrate. No Singular naming-claim or maintenance behaviour exists yet, and
nothing above should be read as evidence that it does.


## Delivered (2026-09-11) — release v0.3.0

Published by the pipeline from annotated tag `v0.3.0` → commit `3e1cf14`:
`singular-onchain-0.3.0.tar.gz` (sha256 `cce0cdb8e4035d6da6284def64c7a270f8541d1a126ff4c1b582e5341e5e463b`)
alongside the continuing documentation archive. Epic 15's `v0.2.0` asset is preserved
unchanged at `acbabdf5…`.

**Verified from the published bytes**, not from this repository: downloaded, checked
against the published `SHA256SUMS`, extracted outside every worktree, 98 members,
internal checksums verified, and all twelve validator entries across both partitions
verified from the archive alone.

### Acceptance criteria

- **Executable ledger cases for canonical bootstrap, certified Insert, permissionless
  fold and exact effects** — `LI01` executes on a devnet with the four-field checkpoint
  decoded from the chain and the representative absence asserted; `LM01` proves
  preservation field by field; the imported cage's fold and request machinery runs under
  the journey and E2E suites. All in CI.
- **Negative cases** — `LI02`, `LI04`, `LI05`, `LI07`, `LI08` refused by validators;
  `LI06` refused by the ledger after a real `LI01`; `LM02`, `LM03`, `LM04` and `LC03`
  refused phase-2 with reasons matched; forged identity, tampered certified output and
  missing witness refused on the imported partition. Each attempt well-formed except the
  element under test.
- **Authorized withdrawal of an unfulfilled Insert** — `WR01` round-trips the refund
  recorded at request time; `LC01` is accepted with the approval consumed; `LC02`
  (redirect), `LC03` (attestation only), `LC04` (folded claim) and `LC06` (replay) are
  refused.
- **Authenticated-state verification** — absence, presence and a rejected false claim,
  each against roots read back from the chain.
- **Traceability, and the limits** — every row traces to the accepted epic-15 v0.2.0
  contract (commit `13231f58833b8feb57f4b0f9b1117bfcfba0c07d`, asset `acbabdf5…`), whose
  wire vectors the codec matches byte for byte. Finite fixture evidence is **not**
  presented as proof over arbitrary transactions.

### Release acceptance

A uniquely versioned, retrievable artifact with its exact script identities and
install/run/replay instructions; its journey and checks reproduce from the artifact
through the pipeline; the declared boundary and limits are explicit.

### Findings carried forward

1. **`LI03` is not realisable as a ledger refusal.** A permissionless chain cannot
   prevent a rival registry. Canonicity rests on name derivation — the registry token
   name is SHA-256 of the canonical seed's outRef, and `LI06` shows that seed can never
   be respent. **#18 should bind the canonical name rather than expect a refusal.**
2. **Two validator defects were found only by executing on a ledger, both behind green
   test suites**: `LC04` unenforced because fold preserved the claim's value, and the
   application script's mint and spend purposes disagreeing so no real cancellation
   could be built.
3. **Inherited Aiken discrepancy, recorded and benign**: the blueprint is built by
   `v1.1.21+unknown` while `aiken.toml` declares `v1.1.16`; a real 1.1.16 binary
   produces the same three hashes.

### Not claimed

Recovery and retirement belong to #17. Consumer conformance belongs to #18. Scalus
(#14) remains deferred. Generic registry `Delete` is preserved in the model while the
naming profile prohibits Delete and reuse.

## Goal

Release the first concrete M1 artifact: a playable M1-specific naming/consumer simulator inside the docs and a frozen, independently verified contract/model/scenario package. The existing published generic registry simulator is a foundation; it allows generic Delete and is not the agreed naming demo or M1 completion evidence.

## P1 user story

As an M1 reviewer, I obtain one versioned release, play claim/maintenance/recovery/permanent retirement in the docs, and reproduce the exact agreed consumer-contract scenarios and rejection cases.

## Architectural invariants

- One canonical registry per application must be established by a concrete initialization mechanism; deterministic policy identity alone is insufficient.
- Registry uniqueness uses MPF; application checkpoint state remains in the representative-NFT-bearing application UTxO. Script/policy roles and their bindings are explicit.
- Certification proves allowed construction and initial state, not identity, entitlement to a spelling or ownership of a payment destination. Approval never reserves a key; Insert checks absence at fold.
- Creating an output does not execute its receiving spending script. Each obligation names the actually executing witness.

- Naming rejects Delete/release/reuse in executable transitions, not just in its menu. Generic Delete remains separately available where required by the core/consumer contract.
- Existing operator-owned #10 is not duplicated or taken over. The imported MPFS baseline is not evidence that Singular behavior is implemented.

## Child tickets, in order

1. #20 — Make M1 naming claims playable in the docs
2. #21 — Simulate payment-address maintenance and withdrawal of pending claims
3. #22 — Simulate recovery through the committed next control address
4. #23 — Simulate owner-or-quorum permanent naming retirement
5. #24 — Make concrete registry and cardano-keri contract scenarios executable
6. #25 — Publish the independently verified M1 simulator and contract release

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A versioned, jointly coordinated consumer contract names cardano-keri's exact required operations, transaction inputs/outputs, datum/redeemer and token shapes, policy/script bindings, witnesses, custody and rejection cases; unresolved consumer details block dependent implementation.
- [ ] Executable positive/negative scenarios establish single initialization, registry authenticity, cross-registry substitution rejection and representative uniqueness under the concrete design.
- [ ] Canonical key/address encodings, hash/domain separation, next-address commitments, bootstrap, request-token lifecycle, application certification, exact withdrawal authorization/refunds and test execution strategy are decided before corresponding code.
- [ ] Naming-specific models cover optional address maintenance, next-key recovery and current controller OR fixed-quorum permanent retirement; stable invariants are proved and independently checked before implementation. Scope and correspondence to #10 are explicit, with no duplicated generic proof ticket.
- [ ] Generic Delete and any additional consumer requirements are explicitly classified and preserved; naming-only restrictions cannot silently narrow the consumer contract.

- [ ] The M1 profile demonstrates claim, optional destination set/replace/clear, authorized pending Insert withdrawal, precommitted recovery, current-owner OR fixed-quorum irrevocable retirement, pending-versus-Over observation and permanent name refusal. Positive and negative traces agree with the frozen model; generic Delete cannot bypass the naming restriction.
- [ ] The docs publish the actual M1-specific simulator with candidate-bound live preview while under review and an accepted-release entry point after acceptance. Operator play findings are resolved; the generic simulator is clearly distinguished from this release.
- [ ] A versioned, retrievable release includes stable/proved model/contracts, runnable naming and agreed consumer scenarios, install/run/replay instructions, exact identities and independent boundary acceptance. Required unresolved proof/contract decisions prevent release acceptance.
- [ ] Each child extends the same artifact, is integrated in the declared order, and preserves earlier runnable journeys. Successor #16 consumes the exact accepted release. Epic #15 owns its CI/release path; packaging does not wait for #18.

## Parallelization and process

The six children are serial because they share the model, browser profile and release artifact. They are vertical observable simulator/contract increments. No parallel implementation or new worker is authorized by this decomposition. Future epic/ticket owners may refine disjoint slice ownership only through a recorded plan; changes to shared contracts or files force serialization. One release inside M1: the M1 docs simulator and executable contract/model scenario package. Bind actual version, artifact format, distribution and replay commands at commissioning. Source/model/browser evidence is distinguished from compiled on-chain and ledger evidence; Singular on-chain behavior is implemented and accepted through later release epics. #16 extends this exact accepted release; #17 and #18 retain their current scope and dependencies.

Start with #20. There is no dependency on source import #19 or deferred Scalus #14. Copying belongs to successor #16. Concrete bootstrap, encodings/hash commitments, witness bindings, request-token/refund rules and actual cardano-keri transaction requirements are settled and verified in the relevant contract slices. Do not guess consumer rules or reopen #10.

Copy ticket #19 belongs to successor epic #16, where validators and existing Haskell transaction/devnet support are needed for ledger implementation. It is not a prerequisite or artifact of this model/contract/simulator release. The indexer remains excluded.

## Inherited boundary and non-goals

M1 serves the agreed cardano-keri on-chain consumer contract; naming is its bounded test application. A model simulation does not establish ledger implementation acceptance. Preserve operator-owned generic foundation #10; any new model/theorem scope is distinct and coordinated. ## Goal

The Lean model on `feat/model-simulation-s1` (PR #3) states 41 theorems in `lean/Singular/Statements.lean`, every one admitted with `sorry`. Prove all of them against the frozen `Model.lean` without changing any statement, and turn the theorem manifest from an inventory of intentional holes into a register of proved declarations backed by a compiled axiom check.

## P1 user story

As a proof reviewer, I run `just model` and observe every declaration in the theorem manifest reported PROVED, the build refusing any declaration that still depends on `sorryAx`, and no `sorry` left in the Lean sources.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `lean/Singular/Statements.lean` contains no `sorry`; every theorem carries a proof.
- [ ] `lean/Singular/Model.lean` is byte-identical to the base branch; no definition is touched to make a proof go through.
- [ ] Every record in `lean/theorem-debt.json` keeps its qualified name and `statementSha256`; status moves to PROVED and debt to none.
- [ ] `lake build` fails when any declaration of `Singular.Statements` depends on `sorryAx` or on a non-standard axiom (control: re-admitting one theorem makes the build red).
- [ ] `tools/check_model.py` still rejects `axiom`, `admit`, `unsafe` and unlisted declarations, and verifies the manifest against the sources.
- [ ] `docs/theorems.md` and every page claiming admitted statements report the proved status; presentation gate passes.
- [ ] `nix develop --quiet -c just ci` is green locally and CI is green on the PR.

## Non-goals

- Changing any theorem statement, definition, or the executable corpus.
- Adding new theorems (for example the missing whole-transition custody-completion statement named in `docs/theorems.md`).
- Running the mutant campaign; the ledger stays a description of the method.
- Merging PR #3; this work stacks on its branch.

## Parent

Stacks on PR #3 (`feat/model-simulation-s1`).
